title: Carry only the useful history
subtitle: Running optima and information from both sides
why: Array scans become useful interview tools when you can explain exactly what information each position needs.
objectives: Derive a best-segment-ending-here invariant.
Combine prefix and suffix information without division.
Separate local state from the final answer.

lesson.title: Extend or restart
lesson.body: For a maximum-sum segment ending at the current value, either extend the previous segment or start here. An earlier negative contribution can only hurt the new segment.

lesson.title: Two directions, one answer
lesson.body: To exclude one value from a product, combine the product strictly before it with the product strictly after it. Store one direction in the answer array and carry the other in a scalar.

lesson.title: State before code
lesson.body: Write what each variable means before and after processing an index. This catches the common mistake of mixing a best result anywhere with a result forced to end here.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.brief: Return the largest sum of a nonempty contiguous segment; values may be negative.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
hints: Track the best segment that must end at each index.
Compare starting at a[i] with extending the previous segment.
Update a separate global best after each local transition.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.brief: Return each position’s product excluding itself, without division; zeros may occur.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(1) extra space excluding output
hints: Ask what lies strictly before and after an index.
Write prefix products into the output.
Multiply by a running suffix product in reverse order.

problems.title: Remove Smallest
problems.brief: Repeatedly remove the smaller of two values differing by at most one; decide whether one element can remain.
problems.target: O(n log n) time and O(n) input storage.
hints: Sort the array.
A gap greater than one between consecutive sorted values can never be crossed by a legal removal.
Return YES exactly when every adjacent sorted gap is at most one.

traps: Do not initialize a nonempty maximum-subarray answer to zero.
Two zeros and one zero produce different product behavior.
Keep output-space and auxiliary-space claims separate.

steps: At 1, restart: endingHere becomes 1.
At 4, restart again because extending the previous -2 loses value.
Extend through -1, 2, 1 to obtain 6.
Later values do not exceed the global best of 6.

takeaway: A scan is correct when its carried state describes exactly the past that future choices need.
recall: Explain why a negative prefix can be discarded without looking at later values.
javaTip: Use long when the stated bounds allow sums or products beyond int; do not assume an int input implies an int result.
checklist: Explain both scan invariants aloud.
Test all-negative values and one-element input.
Test product output with zero, one zero, and two zeros.

title: Turn segments into prefix relationships
subtitle: Frequency maps, first occurrences, and transformed values
why: Prefix relationships handle signed values that break the monotonicity required by many sliding windows.
objectives: Count equal prefix differences.
Use a first occurrence when maximizing length.
Choose map values from the question being asked.

lesson.title: Subtract two prefixes
lesson.body: A segment has sum K precisely when currentPrefix minus an earlier prefix equals K. Counting earlier occurrences gives the number of valid segments ending now.

lesson.title: Count versus earliest index
lesson.body: For a count, store frequencies. For a maximum length, retain the earliest matching prefix index. Overwriting an early index discards the longest candidate.

lesson.title: Transform the condition
lesson.body: Replace binary zero with -1 and one with +1. A balanced segment then becomes a zero-sum segment, allowing the same prefix machinery to solve a different-looking question.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.brief: Count all nonempty contiguous segments summing to K; negative values and zeros are allowed.
problems.target: O(n) expected time, O(n) space
hints: Write sum(l..r) using two prefix sums.
Before inserting the current prefix, count earlier prefixes equal to current-K.
Seed the frequency of prefix zero with one.

problems.title: Contiguous Array
problems.brief: Find the longest contiguous binary segment containing equally many zeros and ones.
problems.target: O(n) expected time, O(n) space
hints: Map zero to -1.
Equal prefix sums delimit a balanced segment.
Store the first index for each prefix, including zero at index -1.

problems.title: Ilya and Queries
problems.brief: Answer substring queries asking how many adjacent character pairs are equal inside each inclusive interval.
problems.target: O(n+q) time and O(n) space.
hints: Let pref[i] count equal adjacent pairs among the first i characters.
Add one when character i equals character i-1.
For one-based inclusive [l,r], return pref[r]-pref[l].

traps: Inserting before querying can count an empty segment when K is zero.
Replacing an earliest index shortens future length candidates.
A sum-based shrinking window is not generally valid with negative values.

dryRun.input: Subarray Sum Equals K: nums=[1, -1, 1], K=1
steps: Start with frequency[0]=1.
Prefix 1 finds one earlier zero: count=1.
Prefix 0 finds no earlier -1; its frequency becomes 2.
Prefix 1 finds two earlier zeros: count=3.

takeaway: The map stores frequencies for counting and earliest positions for longest lengths.
recall: Re-derive the equation earlierPrefix=currentPrefix-K without consulting notes.
javaTip: Use HashMap<Long, Integer> for wide prefix sums and a long answer when the number of segments can be quadratic.
checklist: Trace a zero-heavy case with repeated prefixes.
Explain why the empty prefix is seeded.
Implement both map interpretations from a blank file.

title: Make two pointers earn their movement
subtitle: Sorted-value elimination and geometric bounds
why: Two pointers are useful only when moving one boundary eliminates candidates by a provable rule.
objectives: Justify pointer movement rather than guessing it.
Handle duplicate values without duplicate answers.
Recognize when sorting would destroy the problem.

lesson.title: Sorted sums
lesson.body: After fixing one member of a three-value sum, sorting lets two pointers search the remaining pair. If the sum is too small, only increasing the left value can help.

lesson.title: Dominated containers
lesson.body: For a water container, width shrinks whenever a pointer moves. Keeping the shorter wall while moving the taller one cannot improve the limiting height, so discard the shorter wall.

lesson.title: Preserve meaning
lesson.body: Sorting is valid when only selected values matter. Container indices encode physical distance; sorting the heights changes the question and invalidates the result.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.brief: Return all distinct value triplets whose sum is zero; indices in a triplet must differ.
problems.target: O(n²) time after sorting
hints: Fix one value and search for its complementary pair.
Move pointers according to whether the sorted sum is too small or too large.
Skip duplicate anchors and duplicate pair values after recording a match.

problems.title: Container With Most Water
problems.brief: Choose two original positions maximizing min(height[i],height[j]) times their distance.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(1) space
hints: Begin with the widest candidate.
Ask which wall currently limits the area.
Move a shorter wall; retaining it cannot yield a better area at a smaller width.

problems.title: Books
problems.brief: Find the largest number of consecutive books whose positive reading times fit within the available time.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Expand the right endpoint while adding its reading time.
While the sum exceeds the limit, remove books from the left.
After restoring validity, update the maximum window length.

traps: Deduplicate answers by value, not merely by index.
Do not sort the container heights.
Promote before multiplication or addition when bounds require it.

steps: Anchor -4 produces no valid pair.
Anchor -1 finds [-1,-1,2], then [-1,0,1].
Skip the next identical anchor -1.

takeaway: Each pointer move should eliminate a set of candidates that cannot improve the answer.
recall: Give a counterexample showing why sorting breaks the container problem.
javaTip: Arrays.sort mutates the input; clone it when a caller needs original order later.
checklist: Write the elimination argument for both problems.
Test repeated zeros and repeated anchors.
Trace pointer moves without skipping a valid pair.

title: Reuse prefixes beyond ordinary sums
subtitle: XOR cancellation and modular equivalence
why: Recognizing an algebraic prefix relation avoids treating every array condition as a new algorithm.
objectives: Relate XOR intervals to pairs of prefix XORs.
Count valid split positions using prefix frequency and index sums.
Normalize modulo prefixes when values can be negative.

lesson.title: XOR cancels itself
lesson.body: If prefix XORs at two boundaries are P and Q, their segment XOR is P XOR Q. A desired XOR X therefore asks for an earlier prefix equal to current XOR X.

lesson.title: From zero-XOR intervals to split counts
lesson.body: In the triplet exercise, the XOR on the left equals the XOR on the right exactly when their combined interval has XOR zero. Equal prefixes at i and r therefore contribute r-i-1 possible split positions. Keep both the count and the sum of previous indices for each prefix XOR.

lesson.title: Order of operations
lesson.body: The current prefix must query previously seen states before adding itself. This preserves nonempty segments and naturally counts multiple earlier boundaries.

problems.brief: Count triples i < j <= k where XOR of arr[i..j-1] equals XOR of arr[j..k]. Both parts must be nonempty.
problems.target: O(n) expected time and O(n) space using prefix-XOR counts and index sums.
hints: Equal XORs mean the whole segment arr[i..k] has XOR zero.
Equal prefixes P[i]=P[r] with r=k+1 contribute r-i-1 possible split positions j.
At prefix position r add count[P[r]]*(r-1)-sumPositions[P[r]], then record r; initialize prefix zero at position 0.
problems.title: Count Triplets That Can Form Two Arrays of Equal XOR
Subarray Sums Divisible by K
problems.brief: Count nonempty contiguous segments with sum divisible by positive K; array values may be negative.
problems.target: O(n+K) time with a remainder-frequency array
hints: Discard the full prefix value after finding its remainder.
Normalize negative remainders into [0,K).
Count earlier occurrences of the current remainder, seeded with one empty prefix.

problems.title: AGAGA XOOORRR
problems.brief: Merge adjacent array elements by XOR and decide whether at least two equal elements can remain.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: If the total XOR is zero, splitting into two nonempty parts is enough.
Otherwise seek three nonempty consecutive segments, each with XOR equal to the total.
Greedily reset a running XOR whenever it equals the total; find two completed segments before the final element.

traps: Java % may return a negative remainder.
XOR prefix matching uses XOR, not subtraction.
Use long for a count that may reach n(n+1)/2.

steps: The prefix XORs, including the empty prefix, are [0,2,1,0,6,1].
Equal zero prefixes at positions 0 and 3 describe [2,3,1]. It has 3-0-1=2 legal split points.
Equal prefixes of value 1 at positions 2 and 5 describe [1,6,7]. It also has 5-2-1=2 split points.
No other equal-prefix pairs contribute. Add the two contributions.

takeaway: Find the relation between boundary states before selecting the data structure.
recall: Compare the required earlier prefix for sum K, XOR X, and divisibility by K.
javaTip: Normalize a wide running sum with (int)((sum % k + k) % k), or maintain an already normalized remainder safely.
checklist: I can explain why an equal-prefix pair contributes interval length minus one split points.
Test zeros and repeated prefix states.
Test negative values in the divisibility problem.

title: Compress arithmetic information
subtitle: GCD states and windows over prime factors
why: Arithmetic constraints can still reduce to small state sets or monotone windows when their structure is made explicit.
objectives: Compress repeated GCD outcomes from earlier subarrays.
Factor values without constructing their product.
Deduplicate prime factors across the array.

lesson.title: GCD states collapse
lesson.body: When a value is appended, every previous ending-segment GCD becomes gcd(old,value). Merge equal new GCDs with their counts; many segment lengths collapse into the same arithmetic state.

lesson.title: Factor once, update often
lesson.body: A smallest-prime-factor sieve supports repeated factorizations. A window needs each value’s distinct prime factors, not the multiplicity of a prime within that one value.

lesson.title: A product’s primes form a union
lesson.body: A prime divides the product exactly when it divides at least one array value. Factor each positive value, divide out all copies of each found prime, and add the prime to a set. This avoids product overflow and counts each prime once.

problems.title: Number of Subarrays With GCD Equal to K
problems.brief: Count contiguous segments whose GCD equals positive K; all array values are positive.
problems.target: O(nD log A) time, O(D) rolling states; D is the distinct ending-GCD count
hints: Track GCDs of segments ending at the previous position.
Extend each state with gcd(state,value) and add the singleton segment.
Merge identical GCDs and add the count associated with K.

problems.brief: Count distinct prime factors in the product of positive array values. Factor each value separately; do not construct the product.
problems.target: O(n sqrt(M)) time with trial division; space proportional to the number of distinct primes.
hints: The primes dividing a product are the union of primes dividing each factor.
For each value, try divisors while divisor*divisor <= remaining and remove all copies of a found factor.
Add any remaining value greater than 1 to a HashSet<Integer>; return its size.
problems.title: Distinct Prime Factors of Product of Array
GCD Compression
problems.brief: From 2n integers, choose n-1 disjoint index pairs so the GCD of their pair sums exceeds one.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space.
hints: Separate indices of odd and even values.
Pair indices within each parity group so every pair sum is even.
There are at least n-1 such pairs; print any n-1 and leave two indices unused.

traps: The value 1 contributes no prime factors.
A repeated factor such as 2 in 8 is one distinct factor for that element.
A GCD state needs a frequency, not just membership in a set.

steps: The values 2 and 4 contribute only prime 2. The set is {2}.
The values 3 and 7 add two new primes: {2,3,7}.
Factor 10 as 2×5 and add 5. Factor 6 as 2×3; both primes are already present.

takeaway: Compress equal arithmetic outcomes, or exploit monotone coverage, before trying every segment.
recall: Explain why prime multiplicity inside a number differs from prime frequency across a window.
javaTip: Use int arrays for smallest prime factors and coverage counts when the maximum value is bounded; keep the result count long.
checklist: Validate compressed GCD counts against a tiny quadratic dry-run.
Test 1s, repeated prime powers, and an impossible coverage target.
I can factor and deduplicate primes without multiplying the original values.

title: Array checkpoint: choose the invariant
subtitle: Circular segments and earliest-prefix constraints
why: This checkpoint tests whether you can select an invariant from an unfamiliar condition rather than imitate yesterday’s code.
objectives: Reduce circular structure to linear scans.
Enforce a minimum segment length with prefix indices.
Explain a rejected approach before implementing the chosen one.

lesson.title: Two shapes of optimum
lesson.body: A circular maximum segment either stays inside the array or crosses the boundary. A crossing segment is the total sum minus a nonempty interior segment with minimum sum.

lesson.title: Protect nonempty selection
lesson.body: If all values are negative, removing the whole array would produce an invalid empty wraparound candidate. The ordinary maximum-subarray answer handles this case.

lesson.title: Distance between prefixes
lesson.body: A divisible segment of length at least two needs matching remainder prefixes at least two positions apart. Store the earliest index to maximize the available distance.

problems.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
problems.brief: Return the maximum sum of a nonempty circular segment, using each array position at most once.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(1) space
hints: Separate wrapping and nonwrapping solutions.
A wrapping choice excludes a minimum-sum middle segment.
Compare ordinary maximum with total-minus-minimum, guarding the all-negative case.

problems.title: Continuous Subarray Sum
problems.brief: Determine whether an integer array contains a segment of length at least two whose sum is a multiple of positive K.
problems.target: O(n) expected time, O(min(n,K)) space
hints: Matching prefix remainders identify a divisible segment.
A frequency alone cannot establish its length.
Keep the earliest index for every remainder, with remainder zero at index -1.

problems.title: Even-Odd Game
problems.brief: Alice and Bob alternately remove numbers; Alice scores even picks and Bob scores odd picks, with Alice first. Determine the winner under optimal play.
problems.target: O(n log n) time and O(n) input storage.
hints: Sort values descending.
Process turns in that order: Alice adds even values on her turns and Bob adds odd values on his.
Compare long score totals; choosing a wrong-parity value still consumes the turn.

traps: A wrapping candidate must not represent an empty array.
The length-at-least-two rule cannot be checked using only counts.
Overwriting the earliest remainder index can hide valid segments.

steps: Total sum is 7.
Ordinary maximum is 7 from the whole array.
Minimum nonempty segment is [-3], with sum -3.
The wrapping candidate is 7-(-3)=10.
dryRun.answer: 10 from the final 5 followed by the initial 5

takeaway: Translate the extra condition into a precise change to the state or validity rule.
recall: From memory, list when a prefix map should store a count and when it should store an earliest index.
javaTip: Write tiny local brute-force checkers for practice inputs, but keep judge output limited to the required answer.
checklist: Solve both without looking at previous implementations.
Explain the all-negative guard with [-3,-2,-5].
Record one recognition error and re-solve that case later.

title: Maintain a valid character window
subtitle: Frequency updates and fixed-size multisets
why: String windows reuse array techniques, but repeated characters make the exact validity invariant especially important.
objectives: Shrink until uniqueness is restored.
Represent an anagram as a frequency signature.
Distinguish variable-length and fixed-length windows.

lesson.title: Restore, then measure
lesson.body: When a new character creates a duplicate, remove characters from the left until the window is unique again. Measure the length only after the invariant holds.

lesson.title: Anagrams ignore order
lesson.body: For lowercase English letters, a 26-count vector completely describes a character multiset. A fixed-size window is a permutation exactly when its vector matches the pattern.

lesson.title: Update both boundaries
lesson.body: Every character entering and leaving must affect the maintained state once. If you track a mismatch count instead of comparing vectors, update it around each frequency change.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.brief: Return the maximum length of a contiguous substring with no repeated character.
problems.target: O(n) expected time
hints: Maintain a unique window.
A duplicate requires moving the left edge until its earlier occurrence is excluded.
With last-seen indices, set left=max(left,lastSeen+1).

problems.title: Permutation in String
problems.brief: For lowercase English strings, determine whether the second contains a contiguous permutation of the first.
problems.target: O(n+26) time, O(26) space
hints: All candidate windows have the pattern’s length.
Compare character counts rather than sorted substrings.
Slide by adding one character and removing one character.

problems.title: File Name
problems.brief: Delete the fewest characters from a filename so it contains no substring xxx.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Track the current run length of x.
Every x beyond the second in its run requires one deletion.
Reset the run when a different character appears.

traps: A last-seen jump must never move left backward.
A repeated pattern letter needs its full multiplicity.
A pattern longer than the text has no valid window.

steps: After a,b, the valid window is "ab" with length 2.
The second b moves left beyond the first b.
The final a was last seen before left, so left stays put.
The final window "ba" also has length 2.

takeaway: A window answer is meaningful only after its character-count invariant is restored.
recall: Explain why left=lastSeen+1 alone fails on "abba".
javaTip: A char is a UTF-16 code unit; use a 26-entry array only when the problem explicitly limits input to lowercase English letters.
checklist: Trace "abba" and a repeated-letter pattern.
State the window validity rule before each loop.
Avoid constructing or sorting every candidate substring.

title: Count what a window still needs
subtitle: Minimum cover and distinct-character constraints
why: Coverage and distinct-count questions share the same boundaries but use different definitions of validity.
objectives: Track unmet target frequencies for a covering window.
Count starts that contain a, b, and c using last-seen indices.
Distinguish shortest valid windows from counting every valid window.

lesson.title: Coverage is not uniqueness
lesson.body: A window covers a target when every required count is met. Extra copies and unrelated characters are allowed; they matter only when shrinking exposes a missing requirement.

lesson.title: Shrink while successful
lesson.body: For a minimum cover, record a valid window and keep removing its leftmost character until coverage breaks. This visits the shortest valid candidate for each right boundary.

lesson.title: Count all valid starts from last occurrences
lesson.body: For a string over a, b, and c, fix a right endpoint and keep the most recent index of each letter. A start at or before the minimum of those three indices includes all three letters. Add minimumLastIndex+1; initializing last indices to -1 contributes zero until every letter appears.

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.brief: Return the shortest substring covering every character of the target with its required multiplicity, or an empty string if impossible.
problems.target: O(n+m) time with bounded-alphabet counts
hints: Track how many target character occurrences remain missing.
Adding a useful occurrence reduces what is missing.
When nothing is missing, repeatedly record and shrink until a required occurrence is lost.

problems.brief: For a string containing only a, b, and c, count substrings that contain all three characters at least once.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
hints: Fix the right endpoint and ask which starting positions include all three letters.
Track the most recent index of a, b, and c; initialize every index to -1.
At each right endpoint add 1 + the minimum of the three last-seen indices. Missing characters naturally contribute zero.
problems.title: Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters
They Are Everywhere
problems.brief: Find the shortest substring containing every distinct character present anywhere in the given string.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(alphabet size) space.
hints: Count the distinct characters required by the whole string.
Expand a frequency-counted window until it covers all required characters.
Shrink while coverage remains complete, recording the shortest length.

traps: Distinct target letters do not capture target multiplicities.
K=0 permits only the empty window.
Measure a minimum cover before removing the character that breaks it.

steps: The first complete cover is "ADOBEC".
Later characters restore coverage after earlier requirements are removed.
At the final C, shrink past unnecessary characters.
Removing B from "BANC" would break coverage.

takeaway: Define validity in counts, then choose whether to shrink while valid or while invalid.
recall: Compare the shrinking condition for minimum cover and longest at-most-K substring.
javaTip: Store the best start and length, then create the final substring once instead of allocating one at every improvement.
checklist: Test target="AABC" with repeated required A.
Test impossible coverage and K=0.
Explain why each boundary advances at most n times.

title: Spend a nonnegative window budget
subtitle: Position costs and majority-character replacement
why: Many apparent string-transformation tasks become linear windows when extending a candidate only adds nonnegative cost.
objectives: Convert paired characters into per-position costs.
Explain why nonnegative costs permit shrinking.
Derive the replacement cost of a uniform window.

lesson.title: Aligned transformations
lesson.body: When positions are fixed, transforming one substring into the aligned substring costs the sum of independent character costs. This is a nonnegative subarray-budget problem.

lesson.title: Keep the majority
lesson.body: To make a window uniform, keep its most frequent character and replace all others. The required changes equal window length minus the largest frequency.

lesson.title: Prefer a clear invariant
lesson.body: For a 26-letter alphabet, recomputing the largest frequency during validity checks is still linear with a small constant. Learn the exact invariant before using a stale-maximum optimization.

problems.title: Get Equal Substrings Within Budget
problems.brief: Find the longest aligned substring whose total absolute character-code difference between two equal-length strings is at most maxCost.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
hints: Convert each aligned pair to a nonnegative cost.
Maintain the sum inside a moving window.
Shrink while cost exceeds the budget, then record the length.

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.brief: For an uppercase English string, find the longest substring that can become one repeated letter using at most K replacements.
problems.target: O(26n) with exact frequency checks; O(n) with a justified optimized invariant
hints: The most frequent letter is the cheapest one to preserve.
Required changes equal windowLength-maxFrequency.
Shrink while that cost exceeds K, maintaining an exact maximum initially.

problems.title: Vasya and String
problems.brief: For a string of a and b, find the longest substring that can become all one character with at most k changes.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Run one window targeting a and another targeting b.
Count characters in the window that differ from the target.
Shrink while mismatches exceed k, then maximize the valid length.

traps: Budget zero still permits zero-cost characters.
The equal-substrings problem compares aligned positions, not arbitrary substring pairs.
A stale maximum can invalidate a claimed per-window explanation even when a specialized length algorithm is correct.

steps: The costs are [1,1,1,2].
The first three positions cost 3 and give length 3.
Adding the last position raises cost to 5.
Remove two leading costs to restore a valid cost of 3.

takeaway: A budget window is justified by nonnegative incremental costs and a precisely defined replacement rule.
recall: Explain why negative costs would break ordinary sum-based shrinking.
javaTip: Use a long running cost for custom variants with large weights, even if every individual weight fits int.
checklist: Derive the uniform-window cost formula.
Test budget zero and budget larger than the total.
Explain exact-frequency correctness before attempting the optimization.

title: Choose a stable character signature
subtitle: Grouping anagrams and tracking all anagram windows
why: A canonical signature converts a relationship between whole strings into equality between compact keys.
objectives: Build unambiguous frequency-based keys.
Group equivalent strings without pairwise comparisons.
Return every matching window without repeated sorting.

lesson.title: Canonical representation
lesson.body: Anagrams share the same counts for every letter. A signature must preserve all 26 counts in a fixed order, so equal signatures mean equal multisets.

lesson.title: Key equality matters
lesson.body: The map must compare signature contents rather than object identity. Delimit counts if encoding them as text; otherwise different sequences of counts may produce the same key.

lesson.title: One signature moves
lesson.body: For a text window of fixed length, add the incoming letter and remove the outgoing letter. Comparing 26 entries per window remains linear in text length for this bounded alphabet.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.brief: Group lowercase English strings so each group contains exactly the strings with equal letter multiplicities.
problems.target: O(total characters + 26 × word count) time
hints: Assign each word a canonical frequency signature.
Use that signature as a map key.
Include separators or use a value type with content-based equality.

problems.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
problems.brief: Return every start index where a lowercase text contains a contiguous anagram of the pattern.
problems.target: O(26n+m) time, O(26) working space
hints: Only windows of the pattern length qualify.
Maintain one moving frequency vector.
Record the left boundary whenever all counts match.

problems.title: Letter
problems.brief: Decide whether a letter can be assembled from newspaper characters, ignoring spaces but respecting character case and multiplicity.
problems.target: O(n+m) time and O(alphabet size) space.
hints: Count available non-space characters in the newspaper.
For each non-space letter character, consume one matching character.
Reject a negative remaining count; uppercase and lowercase letters are different.

traps: int[] keys use identity equality in a standard HashMap.
Do not forget the final full window.
An empty word is a valid member of an anagram group when allowed by the input.

steps: Window "cba" at index 0 has counts a=1,b=1,c=1.
Intermediate windows fail because a required count is missing or exceeded.
Window "bac" at index 6 matches again.
Window "acd" at index 7 contains d instead of b.

takeaway: A canonical key must encode the full equivalence condition with reliable content equality.
recall: Why does putting a newly allocated int[26] directly into a HashMap fail to group equal counts?
javaTip: Build a delimited StringBuilder key such as #1#0#2; do not concatenate undecorated decimal counts.
checklist: Test duplicate words and empty strings.
Show two ambiguous undelimited count encodings.
Return every matching index in increasing order.

title: Compare substrings without copying them
subtitle: Prefix hashes, normalization, and collision checks
why: Hashing is a useful extension when many substring comparisons dominate a solution, provided its probabilistic limits are understood.
objectives: Encode a length-10 DNA window exactly with 20 bits.
Separate hash candidates from verified equality.
Identify a monotone condition on duplicate length.

lesson.title: Exact compact codes for a fixed alphabet
lesson.body: DNA has four symbols, so encode each as two bits. A length-10 window fits exactly in 20 bits: shift, append, and mask away old bits. Track codes seen once and already reported. Unlike a general rolling hash, this fixed-length encoding has no collisions.

lesson.title: Candidates, not proof
lesson.body: Different strings can share a hash. Double hashing reduces this risk; direct comparison of candidate ranges establishes equality when an exact result is required.

lesson.title: Search the length
lesson.body: If a duplicate of length L exists, a duplicate of every shorter length also exists. This makes duplicate existence a monotone predicate for binary search; a later phase studies the general pattern.

problems.brief: Return each length-10 substring that occurs more than once in a DNA string over A, C, G, and T, without duplicate answers.
problems.target: O(n) expected time; O(min(n,4^10)) stored fixed-length codes.
hints: There are only four symbols, so a DNA character fits in two bits.
Shift the rolling code by two, append the current symbol, and retain only its lowest 20 bits.
Once ten characters have arrived, track seen codes and add a substring to the answer only on its second occurrence. The 20-bit code is exact, not a probabilistic hash.
problems.title: Repeated DNA Sequences
Longest Duplicate Substring
problems.brief: Return any longest substring occurring at least twice; overlapping occurrences are allowed.
problems.target: About O(n log n) hash work; exact verification adds comparison cost
hints: Write a helper that checks one candidate length.
Use a map from substring hash to earlier start positions.
Binary-search the greatest feasible length and verify candidate matches.

problems.title: Good Substrings
problems.brief: Count distinct substrings containing at most k bad characters, according to a supplied 26-character good/bad mask.
problems.target: O(n^2) time and O(n^2) trie nodes for an exact solution; dense transitions use 26 integers per node.
hints: Start a traversal at every substring start and accumulate its bad-character count.
Stop extending that start once the bad count exceeds k.
Insert valid extensions into a shared substring trie; each newly created node contributes one distinct substring. Use primitive storage to control Java memory.

traps: A hash match is not guaranteed character equality.
Negative modular subtraction must be normalized.
Allowing overlap changes which repeated occurrences qualify.

steps: Length 3 contains "ana" at starts 1 and 3.
These occurrences overlap, which is allowed.
Length 4 has "bana", "anan", and "nana", all distinct.
The greatest feasible length is therefore 3.

takeaway: Hashing makes comparison candidates cheap; correctness still needs a collision strategy.
recall: Explain why duplicate existence is monotone in the requested substring length.
javaTip: Promote multiplication to long before applying a modulus; verify ranges directly instead of allocating every substring.
checklist: I can report repeated DNA sequences once without claiming a general hash is collision-free.
Explain verification cost honestly.
Test a repeated-character string with overlapping matches.

title: String and array checkpoint: count valid windows
subtitle: Exactly-K distinct values and balanced replacement windows
why: Both exercises ask which starts or replacement intervals satisfy a frequency constraint. The data type changes; the window invariant is still the main design decision.
objectives: Count exactly K distinct values through two at-most counts.
Judge a replacement window by frequencies outside it.
Explain why a validity condition permits shrinking.

lesson.title: Subtract neighboring thresholds
lesson.body: Exactly K distinct equals at most K minus at most K-1. Each at-most helper counts right-left+1 valid suffixes after restoring its invariant.

lesson.title: Track the fixed part of a replacement
lesson.body: In Balanced String, letters inside the chosen window may be replaced freely. Keep frequencies outside the window. A window is feasible precisely when every outside count is at most n/4.

lesson.title: Choose the right update rule
lesson.body: Count every valid suffix in the exactly-K exercise. Minimize the length while the outside counts remain feasible in the replacement exercise. A shared two-pointer shape does not mean the answer-update rules are identical.

problems.brief: Count contiguous subarrays containing exactly K distinct integers. Repeated occurrences count as the same distinct value.
problems.target: O(n) expected time and O(n) frequency-map space.
hints: A window with exactly K distinct values is awkward to count directly.
Write an atMost(K) helper and shrink while the distinct count exceeds K.
Each valid right endpoint contributes right-left+1; subtract atMost(K-1) from atMost(K).
problems.title: Subarrays with K Different Integers

problems.brief: For a QWER string whose length is divisible by four, find the shortest substring that can be replaced so every character appears n/4 times.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) frequency space.
hints: Only the characters outside the replacement window are fixed.
A window is feasible when every outside count is at most n/4.
Remove characters from outside counts as the right boundary expands; while feasible, minimize the length and restore characters as the left boundary advances. Return zero if already balanced.
problems.title: Replace the Substring for Balanced String
2-Letter Strings
problems.brief: Count unordered pairs of two-character strings that differ in exactly one position.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(26^2) space.
hints: Maintain counts for each first character, each second character, and each exact pair.
For current (a,b), add first[a]+second[b]-2*exact[a][b].
Query before updating counts and store the pair total in long.

traps: Frequency counts must describe the current window or its outside, not a mixture of both.
Return zero immediately when QWER counts already equal n/4.
Do not count only one substring per right endpoint when several starts are valid.

dryRun.input: Subarrays With K Different Integers: nums=[1,2,1,2,3], K=2
steps: At most two distinct values contributes 1,2,3,4,2 suffixes at successive right endpoints, totaling 12.
At most one distinct value contributes one suffix per right endpoint, totaling 5.
Subtract the counts so only subarrays with exactly two distinct values remain.

takeaway: The validity invariant tells me how to move the boundary; the objective tells me how to update the answer.
recall: Why does a replacement window work when every outside count is at most n/4?
javaTip: Use long both for substring totals and weighted cost sums; keep indices as int.
checklist: I can derive exactly-K as the difference of two at-most counts.
I can maintain outside counts for Balanced String and handle an already balanced input.
I can explain which starts contribute to the count without enumerating every subarray.

title: Search for a boundary, not just a value
subtitle: Lower bounds and rotated sorted ranges
why: A stable binary-search invariant prevents off-by-one failures and extends naturally to answer-space search.
objectives: Find first and last valid positions.
Maintain one consistent interval convention.
Identify the sorted half of a rotated array.

lesson.title: First true position
lesson.body: Lower bound finds the first position meeting a monotone comparison. Use a half-open interval and allow the result to equal n when no position qualifies.

lesson.title: Two boundaries
lesson.body: The first occurrence is a lower bound for target; one past the last is an upper bound. Their difference gives the range length without repeatedly searching equal values.

lesson.title: A sorted half remains
lesson.body: In a rotated strictly increasing array, at least one side of the midpoint is sorted. Test whether the target falls inside that side’s value range before discarding it.

problems.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
problems.brief: Return the first and last positions of a target in a nondecreasing array, or [-1,-1] when absent.
problems.target: O(log n) time, O(1) space
hints: Find the first value at least target.
Find the first value greater than target.
Check that the lower-bound position really contains the target.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.brief: Find a target in a rotated strictly increasing array of distinct integers, or return -1.
problems.target: O(log n) time, O(1) space
hints: Determine which half is sorted.
Compare the target against that half’s endpoints.
Keep the half whose value interval can contain the target.

problems.title: Interesting drink
problems.brief: For each money amount, count shops whose drink price is no greater than that amount.
problems.target: O(n log n+q log n) time and O(n) space.
hints: Sort shop prices once.
Binary-search the first price strictly greater than the query amount.
Its zero-based insertion index equals the affordable-shop count, including duplicate prices.

traps: Do not mix inclusive and half-open endpoint updates.
A lower-bound position is not automatically an exact match.
Distinct values are essential to the clean rotated-half argument.

steps: The first position with value≥8 is index 3.
The first position with value>8 is index 5.
Verify nums[3] equals the target.
Subtract one from the upper bound for the last occurrence.

takeaway: Every binary-search update must preserve the statement about where the boundary can still be.
recall: State your interval convention and terminating condition before writing a loop.
javaTip: Compute mid as lo+(hi-lo)/2; implement upper bound directly instead of searching for target+1, which can overflow.
checklist: Trace an absent target between existing values.
Test an empty array and a single value.
Explain the sorted-half decision on both rotation sides.

title: Recover ordering after rotation
subtitle: Use sorted order for pairs, then recover searchable order after rotation
why: Rotation preserves useful order, but duplicates can erase the evidence needed to discard half of the search range.
objectives: Locate the minimum pivot in a rotated sequence.
Move pair pointers in circular sorted order.
Explain the worst-case cost introduced by duplicates.

lesson.title: Circular sorted order
lesson.body: In a rotated strictly increasing array, the pivot is the smallest value and the previous circular position is the largest. These provide the two ends of a sorted two-pointer search.

lesson.title: Stop before reusing a value
lesson.body: Circular pointer movement follows increasing or decreasing values through modular indices. Stop when the pointers meet so a pair always uses two distinct positions.

lesson.title: Ambiguity costs work
lesson.body: When left, middle, and right values are equal, their values do not reveal the sorted half. Shrinking an endpoint preserves correctness but may reduce the search by only one position.

problems.brief: Find the two distinct positions whose values sum to the target in a nondecreasing array. Return 1-based indices; the problem guarantees one solution.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
hints: Start with one pointer at each end of the sorted array.
If the sum is too small, only moving the left pointer can increase it; if too large, move the right pointer.
Stop on equality and return left+1 and right+1. Do not reuse the same index.
problems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
problems.brief: Determine whether a target occurs in a rotated nondecreasing array that may contain duplicates.
problems.target: O(log n) on informative partitions; O(n) worst case
hints: Check the midpoint before deciding which side is sorted.
Equal boundary values may make the order undecidable.
Safely shrink an ambiguous boundary, otherwise use the sorted-half test.

problems.title: Worms
problems.brief: Given positive worm-pile sizes and one-based worm labels, report which pile contains each queried worm.
problems.target: O(n+q log n) time and O(n) space.
hints: Build increasing cumulative pile sizes.
For a worm label, find the first cumulative size greater than or equal to it.
Return that position plus one; equality belongs to the current pile.

traps: Circular indices must wrap without becoming negative.
A pair cannot use the same position twice.
Claiming guaranteed logarithmic search with arbitrary duplicates is incorrect.

steps: Start with values 6 and 15. Their sum is 21, so move the right pointer left.
Now 6+11=17, still too large. Move the right pointer left again.
Now 6+10=16. Return the two 1-based positions, not the values.

takeaway: Exploit the remaining order, and explicitly account for inputs that hide it.
recall: Construct an all-equal array showing why duplicate rotated search can take linear time.
javaTip: Use (index-1+n)%n for circular decrement and a long sum when values can approach integer limits.
checklist: Trace an unrotated array as a valid rotation.
Test a pair spanning the physical array boundary.
Explain why duplicate ambiguity changes the complexity guarantee.

title: Binary-search a feasible answer
subtitle: Monotone capacity checks and greedy partitioning
why: Some optimization problems become simpler when you test a proposed answer instead of constructing the optimum directly.
objectives: State a monotone feasibility predicate.
Derive safe lower and upper bounds.
Prove the greedy checker used inside the search.

lesson.title: Capacity makes feasibility easier
lesson.body: A larger allowed speed or segment sum cannot make a previously feasible schedule impossible. This gives a false-to-true boundary that binary search can locate.

lesson.title: Greedy contiguous packing
lesson.body: For a proposed maximum segment sum, extend each group as far as possible before starting another. With nonnegative values, ending a group earlier cannot reduce the total number of groups needed.

lesson.title: Exactly versus at most
lesson.body: For positive or nonnegative array values and K≤n, a partition using fewer than K groups can be split into exactly K nonempty groups without increasing its maximum sum. State these conditions.

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.brief: Find the smallest integer speed allowing all piles to be eaten within H hours, with at most one pile worked on per hour.
problems.target: O(n log M) time, where M is the largest pile
hints: Test a fixed speed by summing ceiling divisions.
Higher speed never requires more hours.
Search speeds from 1 through the largest pile.

problems.title: Split Array Largest Sum
problems.brief: Split a nonnegative array into exactly K nonempty contiguous groups and minimize the largest group sum.
problems.target: O(n log S) time, where S is the total sum
hints: Test whether a proposed capacity needs at most K groups.
Greedily fill each group until the next value would exceed capacity.
Search between the largest element and the total sum.

problems.title: Magic Powder - 1
problems.brief: Maximize cookies using ingredient requirements, available supplies, and k units of powder that can replace any missing ingredient.
problems.target: O(n log(U+1)) time and O(n) storage, where U=min_i floor((supply[i]+k)/need[i]).
hints: For x cookies, compute total deficit sum(max(0,x*need[i]-supply[i])).
Feasibility is monotone: x works exactly when the deficit is at most k.
Binary-search the largest feasible x, use long products, and stop summing once the deficit exceeds k.

traps: A checker for contiguous groups must preserve input order.
Negative values invalidate the usual greedy capacity argument.
Ceiling-division sums can overflow int.

steps: Capacity 17 yields [7,2,5], [10], [8]: three groups, so infeasible.
Capacity 18 yields [7,2,5], [10,8]: two groups.
Any capacity below 17 also fails by monotonicity.
The first feasible capacity is 18.

takeaway: Binary search is only as correct as the monotonicity proof and the feasibility checker it repeatedly calls.
recall: Why can an at-most-K checker solve an exactly-K partition problem here?
javaTip: Use long bounds and calculate ceiling division with wide arithmetic, such as (pile+speed-1L)/speed.
checklist: Write the feasibility predicate in one sentence.
Test K=1 and K=n.
Explain the role of nonnegative values in the partition proof.

title: Invert minimum and maximum constraints
subtitle: Spacing placement and consecutive availability
why: Answer search also handles true-to-false predicates, provided the bound updates match the direction of feasibility.
objectives: Search for the last feasible distance.
Use greedy earliest placement to maximize remaining room.
Reset consecutive runs at unavailable positions.

lesson.title: Place early
lesson.body: For a required minimum gap, place each next item at the earliest eligible coordinate. Choosing a later coordinate leaves no more room for future items, so earliest placement is sufficient.

lesson.title: Consecutive availability
lesson.body: At a proposed day, flowers are either available or unavailable. Count consecutive available flowers, forming a bouquet each time a run reaches the required size.

lesson.title: Opposite boundaries
lesson.body: A larger minimum gap is harder to satisfy, while a later bloom day is easier. Write whether you seek the last true or first true value before implementing the search.

problems.brief: Place m balls in distinct basket positions to maximize the minimum distance between any two balls. Positions need sorting first.
problems.target: O(n log n + n log R) time, where R is the coordinate range.
hints: Ask whether a proposed minimum distance d is achievable.
Place the first ball at the leftmost position, then greedily use the next position at least d away.
Feasibility is true for smaller distances and false for larger ones; binary-search the last feasible distance with a progress-safe midpoint.
problems.title: Magnetic Force Between Two Balls
Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets
problems.brief: Find the earliest day to make m nonoverlapping bouquets, each using k adjacent flowers, given their bloom days; return -1 if impossible.
problems.target: O(n log D) time, D is the bloom-day range
hints: Reject immediately if m*k exceeds n.
For a proposed day, count usable consecutive runs.
Reset at an unavailable flower and after completing each bouquet.

problems.title: Poisoned Dagger
problems.brief: Attacks occur at increasing times. Poison deals one damage per second for k seconds after an attack, with a new attack refreshing the effect; find the smallest k that deals at least h total damage.
problems.target: O(n log h) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: For a fixed k, each attack except the last contributes min(k, nextTime-currentTime).
The final attack contributes k; add using long and stop once damage reaches h.
Total damage is nondecreasing in k, so binary-search the first sufficient duration.

traps: Use a last-feasible search for spacing and first-feasible search for bloom day.
Adjacency in the bouquet problem refers to original order.
The product m*k needs wide arithmetic before the impossibility check.

steps: Gap 3 permits placements at 1,4,8.
Gap 4 permits only 1,8, so it fails.
Larger gaps also fail.
The maximum feasible gap is 3.

takeaway: Name the feasible side of the answer boundary before choosing loop updates.
recall: Compare the proof for earliest placement with greedy contiguous packing from Day 15.
javaTip: For a last-true search, an upper midpoint lo+(hi-lo+1)/2 can prevent stalling when assigning lo=mid.
checklist: Prove why later greedy placement cannot help.
Test bouquets separated by one late-blooming flower.
Dry-run a two-value search range to ensure termination.

title: Prove an interval greedy choice
subtitle: Earliest finishes and shared intersection points
why: Interval problems are a good place to practice exchange arguments rather than memorizing a sort order.
objectives: Choose a sort key from the objective.
Explain why an early finishing choice preserves options.
Handle endpoint equality according to the statement.

lesson.title: Finish early
lesson.body: Among overlapping candidates, retaining the interval that ends first leaves the largest possible remaining timeline. Replacing a later-finishing first choice with it cannot reduce future selections.

lesson.title: One point can serve many
lesson.body: For closed balloon intervals, place an arrow at the earliest right endpoint. It hits every interval containing that point; the next unhit interval requires another arrow.

lesson.title: Equality is semantic
lesson.body: Touching job intervals may be compatible, while a balloon ending at x and another beginning at x share an arrow. Translate the problem’s endpoint convention directly into the comparison.

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.brief: Return the minimum number of intervals to remove so the remainder do not overlap; touching endpoints are allowed.
problems.target: O(n log n) time
hints: Maximize how many intervals can be retained.
Sort by finish time.
Keep an interval when its start is at least the previous chosen end.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
problems.brief: Each balloon is a closed interval; find the fewest x-coordinates whose arrows hit every interval.
problems.target: O(n log n) time
hints: Sort balloons by their right endpoint.
Shoot at the first uncovered right endpoint.
Start another arrow only when the next interval begins strictly after the current arrow.

problems.title: Woodcutters
problems.brief: Trees stand at increasing coordinates and may remain standing or fall left or right by their height. Maximize felled trees while their occupied segments do not touch another standing or fallen tree.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space after reading the ordered trees.
hints: Track the rightmost occupied coordinate after processing earlier trees.
Prefer falling left when x-height is strictly beyond that boundary.
Otherwise fall right only if x+height is strictly before the next tree; update the occupied boundary accordingly.

traps: Sorting by interval length does not provide the required guarantee.
Strict versus non-strict comparison changes endpoint behavior.
Subtracting endpoints in a comparator may overflow.

steps: Sort by ending coordinate: [1,6],[2,8],[7,12],[10,16].
An arrow at 6 hits the first two intervals.
The interval [7,12] is uncovered, so shoot at 12.
That second arrow also hits [10,16].

takeaway: A greedy choice needs a reason it preserves a solution at least as good as the alternatives.
recall: Explain the earliest-finish exchange argument without referring to the implementation.
javaTip: Sort int[][] with Integer.compare(a[1],b[1]) rather than a[1]-b[1].
checklist: Test intervals that only touch at endpoints.
Explain the difference between selection and stabbing objectives.
Give a counterexample to sorting only by shortest interval.

title: Search checkpoint: defend the decision rule
subtitle: Shipping capacity and ordered interval insertion
why: This checkpoint combines monotone optimization with order-preserving interval reasoning and asks for explicit correctness arguments.
objectives: Build a capacity checker from the shipping rules.
Insert an interval without unnecessary resorting.
Choose tests that target boundary conventions.

lesson.title: A shipping day is a group
lesson.body: A fixed capacity partitions the ordered packages into contiguous days. Greedily fill a day until the next package would exceed capacity, then start a new day.

lesson.title: Three interval regions
lesson.body: When existing intervals are sorted and nonoverlapping, those strictly before the new interval can be copied. Merge the overlapping region, then append the untouched suffix.

lesson.title: Checkpoint explanation
lesson.body: Before coding, identify which order the input already provides and which property is monotone. The answer should justify every boundary update and merge comparison.

problems.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
problems.brief: Ship packages in their original order within D days; find the minimum daily weight capacity.
problems.target: O(n log S) time, S is total package weight
hints: The capacity must fit the heaviest package.
Count required days by greedily filling each day.
Binary-search the first capacity needing no more than D days.

problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.brief: Insert a new closed interval into sorted nonoverlapping closed intervals, merging all overlaps and retaining sorted order.
problems.target: O(n) time plus output space
hints: Copy intervals completely before the new one.
Expand the new interval while overlap continues.
Append the merged interval and then the remaining suffix.

problems.title: Burning Midnight Oil
problems.brief: Vasya first writes v lines, then floor(v/k), floor(v/k²), and so on until the term is zero. Find the smallest v whose total is at least n.
problems.target: O(log n · log_k n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Test v by repeatedly dividing a running term by k and summing the terms.
Avoid computing growing powers of k; integer division directly generates each contribution.
A larger v never produces fewer lines, so binary-search v from 1 through n.

traps: Shipping may use fewer than D days.
Closed intervals sharing an endpoint overlap for this merge task.
If input is already ordered, sorting again may be unnecessary.

steps: [1,3] overlaps the new interval.
Expand the merged interval to [1,5].
[6,9] begins after the merged end and remains unchanged.
Append the merged interval before the untouched suffix.

takeaway: Preserve useful input order and make the condition for each structural change explicit.
recall: Compare the endpoint rule here with the compatible touching jobs from Day 17.
javaTip: Allocate new interval arrays for output when mutating the caller’s interval objects would be surprising.
checklist: Solve both without consulting a saved template.
Test a new interval that absorbs every existing interval.
Write a short proof of the shipping checker’s minimum-day count.

title: Let a stack remember unresolved boundaries
subtitle: Next-greater events and histogram spans
why: A monotonic stack avoids repeatedly scanning forward by resolving waiting indices only when their answer becomes known.
objectives: Store indices whose next greater value is unresolved.
Define when equal values should be popped.
Derive rectangle width from exclusive boundaries.

lesson.title: An unresolved promise
lesson.body: For warmer temperatures, the stack holds indices waiting for a strictly greater value. A new temperature resolves every smaller value on top before its own index is pushed.

lesson.title: A smaller bar closes a span
lesson.body: In a histogram, popping a taller bar fixes the first smaller boundary to its right. The remaining stack identifies its smaller boundary to the left, determining its maximal width.

lesson.title: Amortized work
lesson.body: A nested while loop does not imply quadratic time here. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total number of stack operations is linear.

problems.title: Daily Temperatures
problems.brief: For each day, return how many days must pass before a strictly warmer temperature; return zero if none exists.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(n) space
hints: Keep indices still waiting for warmer weather.
When the current value is larger, pop waiting indices and record the distance.
Leave unresolved indices with answer zero.

problems.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
problems.brief: Return the largest rectangle area formed by consecutive unit-width bars of nonnegative heights.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(n) space
hints: A rectangle can be identified by its limiting bar height.
A smaller incoming bar closes spans for taller stack entries.
After popping j at index i, width is i-leftSmaller-1; flush remaining bars with a sentinel.

problems.title: Alternating Current
problems.brief: Determine whether the sequence of '+' and '-' signs can be completely reduced by repeatedly deleting two adjacent equal signs, the cancellation criterion for the original wire problem.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) stack space.
hints: A cancellation can expose a new adjacent pair across the removed positions.
Keep unresolved signs in a stack; pop when the next sign equals the top, otherwise push it.
The reduction succeeds exactly when the stack is empty after the full scan.

traps: Daily Temperatures requires strictly warmer, not equal.
Histogram widths exclude both smaller boundaries.
Use one consistent equal-height convention when building spans.

steps: The bar of height 1 closes the initial height-2 span.
Heights 5 and 6 remain open until the next height 2.
Popping 6 gives width 1 and area 6.
Popping 5 gives width 2 and area 10.
Final flushing produces no larger rectangle.

takeaway: A monotonic stack stores unresolved candidates until one event determines their boundary.
recall: Explain why a loop that pops many entries can still produce O(n) total work.
javaTip: Use ArrayDeque<Integer> as a stack with push, peek, and pop instead of the legacy Stack class.
checklist: Trace increasing, decreasing, and equal-height inputs.
Derive the width formula from actual indices.
Explain what remains unresolved at the end and how it is handled.

title: Keep only candidates that can still win
subtitle: Monotonic deques with time and value constraints
why: A deque can discard candidates that are both older and no better, giving linear solutions even when ordinary windows fail.
objectives: Separate expired candidates from dominated candidates.
Maintain maximum candidates by index.
Combine prefix sums with a monotonic deque for signed values.

lesson.title: Expiration at the front
lesson.body: For a fixed-length maximum window, the front candidate is the largest. Remove it when its index falls outside the window; its value alone cannot reveal expiration.

lesson.title: Domination at the back
lesson.body: A newer value at least as large as an older one is preferable for future maximum windows because it expires later. Remove such dominated older values from the back.

lesson.title: Signed-sum candidates
lesson.body: For shortest sum-at-least-K, use prefix sums. A newer prefix no larger than an older prefix dominates it, while any front prefix satisfying the target yields a candidate length and can be removed.

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.brief: Return the maximum value in every contiguous window of a specified positive size K.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(K) space
hints: Store candidate indices rather than just values.
Expire indices outside the window from the front.
Remove smaller or equal candidates from the back before adding the new index.

problems.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
problems.brief: Find the shortest nonempty contiguous segment whose sum is at least positive K; values may be negative, and return -1 if none exists.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(n) space
hints: Convert segment sums into differences of prefix sums.
Remove feasible front prefixes while updating the shortest length.
Remove back prefixes at least as large as the new prefix, because the newer smaller prefix dominates them.

problems.title: Minimal string
problems.brief: Starting with input s and empty strings t and u, repeatedly move the first character of s to the end of t or the last character of t to the end of u. Construct the lexicographically smallest possible u.
problems.target: O(n+σ) time and O(n+σ) space, with σ=26.
hints: The intermediate string t behaves like a stack.
Track the smallest character still unread in s using remaining frequencies or suffix minima.
After pushing a character, pop while the stack top is no greater than the smallest unread character; drain the stack when input is exhausted.

traps: A normal sum-shrinking window is invalid with arbitrary negatives.
For sum differences, include the empty prefix at position zero.
The maximum-window deque must expire by position, even when values repeat.

dryRun.input: Shortest signed segment: nums=[2,-1,2], K=3; prefixes=[0,2,1,3]
steps: Start with prefix index 0.
Prefix 2 is retained after prefix 0.
New prefix 1 removes the older prefix 2 from the back.
Final prefix 3 differs from prefix 0 by 3, giving length 3.
No shorter retained candidate reaches K.

takeaway: Discard a candidate only when a newer one is at least as good for every future endpoint.
recall: Explain why a newer smaller prefix dominates an older larger prefix.
javaTip: Keep prefix sums in long[] and deque indices as integers; mixing value and index types can hide expiration bugs.
checklist: State both deque invariants separately.
Test negative-heavy input with no answer.
Trace equal prefix sums and justify removing the older one.

title: Find structure in a repeated walk
subtitle: Floyd’s meeting point and cycle entry
why: Cycle detection applies to linked pointers and to arrays that define a next-state function.
objectives: Distinguish detecting a cycle from locating its entry.
Derive the two-pointer reset phase.
Model an array as a functional graph without changing it.

lesson.title: Meeting is not entry
lesson.body: A slow pointer advances once while a fast pointer advances twice. If they meet, the meeting point is somewhere in the cycle, not necessarily the cycle’s entry.

lesson.title: Reset one walker
lesson.body: Let the distance to the entry be a and cycle length be c. The meeting relation makes the remaining offset compatible modulo c; moving one pointer from the head and one from the meeting point finds the entry.

lesson.title: An index is a node
lesson.body: When each array value names a valid next index, following nums[index] creates a functional graph. Under the duplicate-number constraints, the reachable cycle entry identifies the repeated value.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle II
problems.brief: Return the node where a singly linked list’s cycle begins, or null if there is no cycle; do not modify the list.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(1) space
hints: First seek a meeting using one-step and two-step walkers.
Reset one pointer to the head after a meeting.
Advance both one step at a time until they meet again.

problems.title: Find the Duplicate Number
problems.brief: An array of n+1 integers contains values in [1,n] with exactly one repeated value, possibly repeated more than twice. Find it without modifying the array and with constant extra space.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(1) space
hints: Treat index i as pointing to nums[i].
The walk from the designated start eventually enters a cycle.
Apply the meeting-and-entry phases consistently using the same start convention.

problems.title: Party
problems.brief: Each employee has at most one direct manager, and the hierarchy contains no cycles. Find the minimum number of groups so no group contains an employee together with any direct or indirect manager.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space with adjacency traversal or memoized chain depths.
hints: Employees along one manager chain must all occupy different groups.
Compute each employee's depth from a top-level manager.
The maximum depth is necessary and sufficient: grouping employees by depth achieves it.

traps: Check fast and fast.next before advancing a linked-list fast pointer.
Compare node identity, not equal stored values.
The duplicate-array argument depends on the stated [1,n] bounds and duplicate structure.

steps: The index walk from 0 is 0→1→3→2→4→2.
Indices 2 and 4 form the reachable cycle.
The cycle begins at index 2, the repeated destination value.
Floyd’s reset phase locates that entry without modifying nums.

takeaway: A repeated-state walk exposes a cycle; a second phase locates where the repetition begins.
recall: Explain why equal values in different linked-list nodes do not establish a cycle.
javaTip: Use reference equality (slow==fast) for ListNode identity; avoid comparing slow.val and fast.val.
checklist: Test no cycle, a self-loop, and entry at the head.
Draw the functional graph for the duplicate example.
Explain the reset phase with distances rather than memorized pointer moves.

title: Rewire lists while preserving access
subtitle: Complete-group reversal and deep copying
why: Pointer tasks become safer when each mutation preserves a named route to the unprocessed data.
objectives: Verify a full group before reversing it.
Reconnect processed and unprocessed regions.
Copy arbitrary references without sharing original nodes.

lesson.title: Four boundaries
lesson.body: For group reversal, name the previous group tail, the current group head, the kth node, and the next group head. Save the suffix before any pointer is overwritten.

lesson.title: Temporary structure can help
lesson.body: For a random-pointer copy, interleave each new node immediately after its original. This places the copy of any original x at x.next while random links are assigned.

lesson.title: Restore the caller’s list
lesson.body: The interleaving method must split the two lists again. Its space benefit relies on restoring every original next pointer and connecting the copied nodes only to copied nodes.

problems.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
problems.brief: Reverse every complete group of K nodes in a singly linked list; leave a final short group unchanged and change links rather than node values.
problems.target: O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space
hints: Use a dummy predecessor for the head.
Locate the kth node before mutating a group.
Reverse toward the saved next-group node, then reconnect both ends.

problems.title: Copy List with Random Pointer
problems.brief: Create a deep copy of a list whose random pointer may target any node or null; the final original list must be unchanged.
problems.target: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space with interleaving, excluding copies
hints: First make an original-to-copy mapping conceptually.
Interleave copies to store that mapping inside next links.
Assign copy.random from original.random.next, then separate and restore both lists.

problems.title: Two Teams
problems.brief: Skills form a permutation along a line. Coaches alternate choosing the highest-skill remaining player and up to k remaining neighbors on each side; output each player's team.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space using descending skills and doubly linked index arrays.
hints: Map every skill to its original index and keep prev/next links between unassigned players.
Process skills in descending order, skipping players already assigned.
Collect the chosen player and up to k current neighbors per side, remove that contiguous block, and alternate the team.

traps: Do not reverse a short final group when the contract says to retain it.
Save the next node before overwriting next.
A copied random pointer must not point back into the original list.

steps: Confirm nodes 1 and 2 form a complete group; save node 3.
Reverse and reconnect to obtain 2→1→3→4→5.
Reverse the complete group 3,4 to obtain 2→1→4→3→5.
Only node 5 remains, so leave it unchanged.

takeaway: Before overwriting a pointer, name the saved reference that keeps every required node reachable.
recall: Why does checking for a complete group after partially reversing it complicate correctness?
javaTip: A dummy ListNode removes head-special-case branches; store node references explicitly instead of hiding pointer mutations in dense expressions.
checklist: Trace K=1 and K larger than the list.
Verify the original random-pointer list is restored.
Check that no copied link refers to an original node.

title: Keep a small frontier in a heap
subtitle: Multiway merging and bounded top-K selection
why: A heap is useful when the next answer must be chosen repeatedly from a changing but limited candidate frontier.
objectives: Represent one frontier node from each sorted source.
Keep only K best candidates when full sorting is unnecessary.
Choose min-heap versus max-heap from the eviction rule.

lesson.title: One representative per list
lesson.body: The smallest unmerged value from a sorted list is its current head. Keeping only these heads in a heap is enough to choose the globally smallest next value.

lesson.title: Evict the weakest retained item
lesson.body: For top-K frequency selection, maintain a min-heap of retained candidates by frequency. When its size exceeds K, removing the smallest preserves the K strongest seen so far.

lesson.title: Count what is in the heap
lesson.body: Merge complexity depends on the number of lists, not total nodes, because the heap contains at most one active node per list. Selection complexity depends on K rather than all distinct values.

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.brief: Merge K individually sorted acyclic linked lists into one sorted list; input lists do not share nodes.
problems.target: O(N log K) time, O(K) heap space
hints: Insert the first node of every nonempty list.
Remove the smallest frontier node and append it.
Insert that node’s successor if it exists.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.brief: Return the K values occurring most frequently in an integer array; any output order is acceptable.
problems.target: O(n+u log K) time, O(u+K) space for u distinct values
hints: Count value frequencies first.
Use a size-K min-heap ordered by frequency.
Evict the least frequent retained candidate whenever size exceeds K.

problems.title: Heap Operations
problems.brief: Insert extra commands into a min-heap operation log so every removeMin and getMin x is valid, while preserving all original commands in order. Output the corrected log.
problems.target: O((n+a) log(n+a)) time and O(n+a) space, where a is the number of inserted commands.
hints: Before getMin x, remove every smaller heap value.
If the heap is then empty or its minimum exceeds x, insert x before preserving the getMin command.
Before an original removeMin on an empty heap, insert any value, then preserve the removal.

traps: Do not insert null list heads.
The heap comparator must compare priority, not accidentally the value itself.
State whether reused nodes are allowed; linked-list merging usually permits rewiring.

steps: Initial heap frontier is 1,1,2.
Taking each 1 exposes successors 4 and 3.
Taking 2 exposes 6; the next minimum is then 3.
Continue replacing each removed node with its successor.

takeaway: A heap should hold the candidates that can become the next answer, not every possible item by default.
recall: Why does the merge heap contain at most K nodes even though the output contains N nodes?
javaTip: Use PriorityQueue<ListNode> with Integer.compare(a.val,b.val), and define explicit tie behavior when reproducibility matters.
checklist: Test all-empty and single-list input.
Explain why top-K uses a min-heap for eviction.
State complexity using N, K, and distinct-value count precisely.

title: Structure checkpoint: synchronize two invariants
subtitle: Recency order and greedy heap scheduling
why: More realistic data-structure questions require a map or heap to stay consistent with a second ordering rule.
objectives: Maintain lookup and recency together.
Remove and reinsert nodes without stale map entries.
Schedule repeated characters while preventing adjacent equality.

lesson.title: Two views of one cache
lesson.body: An LRU cache needs a map for direct lookup and a doubly linked list for recency. Every successful access moves the corresponding node to the most-recent end.

lesson.title: Hold the previous choice aside
lesson.body: To reorganize characters, choose the most frequent available character while temporarily withholding the character used immediately before. Return that previous character to the heap only after a different one is chosen.

lesson.title: Check feasibility first
lesson.body: No arrangement can separate a character appearing more than ceil(n/2) times. This bound provides an early rejection and a useful correctness check for the produced schedule.

problems.title: LRU Cache
problems.brief: Implement get and put with positive capacity; successful gets and writes make a key most recent, and excess capacity evicts the least recently used key.
problems.target: O(1) average time per operation, O(capacity) space
hints: Use a HashMap from key to list node.
Use a doubly linked list with dummy endpoints for recency.
Move on access and delete the same evicted key from both structures.

problems.title: Reorganize String
problems.brief: Rearrange a lowercase string so no equal letters are adjacent, or return an empty string if impossible.
problems.target: O(n log σ) time, O(σ) working space
hints: Count letters and test the maximum-frequency bound.
Use a max-heap for available letters.
Hold the previously chosen letter outside the heap until a different letter is appended.

problems.title: Registration System
problems.brief: Process requested names made of lowercase letters. Print OK for a name's first registration; for a repeated name, print the original name followed by the smallest positive integer suffix that makes the registration unique.
problems.target: O(total input/output characters) expected time with hashing; O(n) stored names and counters.
hints: Store the next suffix to use for each requested base name.
For a new base name, print OK and initialize its next suffix to 1.
For a repeated base, append its current suffix and increment the counter; the original lowercase-only input rule makes generated digit suffixes distinct.

traps: Updating an existing cache key should not create a second list node.
Eviction must remove both the list node and its map entry.
Returning the previous character too soon permits equal neighbors.

dryRun.input: LRU capacity=2: put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2)
steps: After the two puts, key 1 is least recent.
get(1) returns 1 and moves key 1 to most recent.
put(3,3) evicts key 2.
get(2) therefore misses; recency remains 3 then 1.
dryRun.answer: get(1)=1; get(2)=-1; retained keys are 1 and 3

takeaway: When two structures represent the same objects, each operation must preserve both views atomically at the algorithm level.
recall: List every link and map update needed to evict one cache entry.
javaTip: For learning, implement the HashMap-plus-doubly-linked-list design explicitly before comparing it with LinkedHashMap access-order mode.
checklist: Test repeated writes to one key at capacity 1.
Verify every reorganized result preserves original letter counts.
State and check both invariants after each cache operation.

title: Draw the choices before writing recursion
subtitle: Subset trees, combination bounds, and duplicate control
why: Recursion becomes manageable when every call has a precise remaining-choice set and each root-to-leaf path has a clear meaning.
objectives: Define the start index as the remaining-choice boundary.
Distinguish same-depth duplicates from valid repeated values.
Prune when too few candidates remain.

lesson.title: A path is a partial answer
lesson.body: A call’s path contains chosen elements, while start identifies which later indices remain available. Advancing start prevents reusing an index and avoids generating reordered copies of one combination.

lesson.title: Duplicates belong to a depth
lesson.body: After sorting, skip a repeated value when its earlier equal copy was already considered at the same depth. The same value can still appear deeper in the path through a different input index.

lesson.title: Count the remaining slots
