lesson.body: If the path needs r more choices and fewer than r candidates remain, that branch cannot finish. Tightening the loop’s final starting position implements this bound directly.

problems.title: Subsets II
problems.brief: Return every distinct subset of an integer array that may contain duplicate values, including the empty subset.
problems.target: O(n·2^n) output-sensitive upper bound
hints: Sort to place equal candidates next to each other.
Record the current path at every call.
Skip nums[i]==nums[i-1] only when i is beyond the current call’s start.

problems.title: Combinations
problems.brief: Return all ways to choose K distinct numbers from 1 through N; ordering within a choice is irrelevant.
problems.target: O(K·C(N,K)) output work plus traversal
hints: Keep choices increasing by passing the next start value.
The remaining number of slots determines whether a branch can finish.
Stop candidate starts at N-remainingSlots+1.

problems.title: Preparing Olympiad
problems.brief: Choose at least two problems whose difficulty sum lies in [l,r] and whose maximum minus minimum difficulty is at least x. Count all valid index subsets.
problems.target: O(n·2^n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for direct mask enumeration.
hints: Enumerate subsets and reject masks containing fewer than two indices.
For each remaining mask, compute its sum, minimum, and maximum.
Count it only when l<=sum<=r and maximum-minimum>=x; equal difficulties at different indices are still different choices.

traps: Globally skipping repeated values loses valid subsets such as [2,2].
Store a copy of the path, not the mutable path object.
Prune based on remaining candidates, not merely current depth.

steps: Record the empty subset.
Under the branch starting with 1, record [1], [1,2], and [1,2,2].
At the root, the first 2 starts [2] and [2,2].
Skip the second root-level 2 because it would repeat those same branches.

takeaway: A recursive call should make its remaining choices and the meaning of its path unambiguous.
recall: Explain why duplicate skipping uses i>start rather than simply i>0.
javaTip: Save results with new ArrayList<>(path), and undo a choice with path.remove(path.size()-1).
checklist: Draw the first two levels of the state-space tree.
Test all-equal input and K=N.
Explain every duplicate branch that is skipped.

title: Make duplicate permutations impossible
subtitle: Used indices and frequency-state recursion
why: Permutation problems allow every unused candidate at each depth, so duplicate control must match that different choice structure.
objectives: Track which input positions are already used.
Use frequencies when equal copies are interchangeable.
Count nonempty prefixes without storing every generated string.

lesson.title: Order changes the result
lesson.body: Unlike combinations, permutations allow remaining candidates from any index. A used array marks membership in the current path while depth determines the next output position.

lesson.title: Choose equal copies canonically
lesson.body: After sorting, an unused equal copy should not be chosen before its preceding equal copy at the same depth. This assigns one canonical index ordering to otherwise indistinguishable choices.

lesson.title: Counts remove identity
lesson.body: For letter tiles, recurse on remaining character frequencies. Choosing one available letter creates one new nonempty sequence, then recursion counts all its extensions.

problems.title: Permutations II
problems.brief: Return all distinct full-length permutations of an integer array that may contain duplicates.
problems.target: O(n·n!) worst-case output-sensitive time, O(n) recursion state
hints: Sort and use a boolean used array.
At each position, try every unused index.
Skip an equal index when its previous equal index is not currently used.

problems.title: Letter Tile Possibilities
problems.brief: Given a multiset of uppercase letter tiles, count all distinct nonempty sequences using each physical tile at most once.
problems.target: Output-state-dependent exponential time; O(σ+n) recursion state
hints: Equal tiles need counts, not separate identities.
For each positive count, consume one letter.
Add one for this prefix plus the recursive extension count, then restore the frequency.

problems.title: Permutations
problems.brief: Given n digit strings of the same length k, apply one shared permutation of digit positions to every string. Minimize the difference between the largest and smallest resulting numeric values; leading zeros are allowed.
problems.target: O(k!·n·k) time and O(k) permutation-generation space, excluding the stored input.
hints: The permutation rearranges columns, not the list of numbers.
Generate each permutation of positions 0 through k-1 exactly once.
Build every transformed value under that permutation, then update the minimum of maxValue-minValue.

traps: A combination start-index restriction would miss valid permutations.
Restore both path and used/frequency state after a branch.
The tile problem counts partial nonempty sequences, not only full-length permutations.

steps: One-letter sequences are A and B.
Two-letter sequences are AA, AB, and BA.
Three-letter sequences are AAB, ABA, and BAA.
Equal A tiles do not create separate copies of the same sequence.

takeaway: Use index identity only when it matters; frequency states naturally remove interchangeable-copy duplication.
recall: Compare the duplicate-skip condition for subsets with the one for permutations.
javaTip: An int[26] frequency array is a compact recursive state for a bounded uppercase alphabet; restore the exact entry before returning.
checklist: Trace [1,1,2] and identify the three unique permutations.
Explain why the tile count includes shorter prefixes.
Check state restoration after the last branch at each depth.

title: Prune positive-sum branches safely
subtitle: Reusable candidates versus one-time candidates
why: A one-line change to the next index changes the legal search space; understanding that choice is more valuable than memorizing a template.
objectives: Model remaining target explicitly.
Choose whether a candidate can be reused.
Justify sorted positive-value pruning.

lesson.title: The next index is a rule
lesson.body: Passing i allows the current candidate again, while passing i+1 forbids reuse of its index. This encodes the problem’s usage policy directly in the recursion.

lesson.title: Positivity supports a bound
lesson.body: After sorting positive candidates, if a value exceeds the remaining target, every later value also exceeds it. The entire rest of that loop can be skipped.

lesson.title: Equal choices at one depth
lesson.body: When candidates may repeat but each index is single-use, sort and skip equal choices at the same depth. Equal values selected at later depths can still be necessary.

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.brief: Given distinct positive candidate values and a positive target, return unique combinations summing to the target; each value may be reused any number of times.
problems.target: Exponential output-dependent time; recursion depth bounded by target/minValue
hints: Sort and carry a remaining target.
Keep choices nondecreasing to avoid reordered duplicates.
After choosing index i, recurse from i to allow reuse.

problems.title: Combination Sum II
problems.brief: Given positive candidates that may repeat, return unique target-sum combinations using each input index at most once.
problems.target: O(n·2^n) output-sensitive upper bound
hints: Sort and skip equal candidates at the same depth.
Recurse from i+1 after choosing index i.
Break when a candidate exceeds the remaining target.

problems.title: Petr and a Combination Lock
problems.brief: For every given rotation angle, choose clockwise or counterclockwise. Decide whether using all angles can return the lock to its initial position, meaning the signed sum is divisible by 360.
problems.target: O(2^n) time and O(n) recursion space.
hints: At index i, branch by adding or subtracting angle[i].
Use a state consisting of the next index and current signed angle, optionally normalized modulo 360.
Accept only after every angle is used and the total is congruent to zero modulo 360.

traps: Reusable zero or negative values can destroy termination of the simple positive-target recursion.
Do not use i+1 in the reusable version.
A Set of final answers can hide incorrect duplicate generation rather than fix the search tree.

steps: Choose the first 1, leaving target 2.
A second 1 leaves target 1, which cannot be completed.
Choosing 2 after the first 1 completes [1,2].
Skip the second root-level 1 to avoid generating [1,2] again.

takeaway: Every recursion parameter should encode a rule: remaining demand, legal candidates, or usage constraints.
recall: Explain exactly why the candidate-exceeds-remaining break requires sorted positive values.
javaTip: Keep result construction separate from recursion-state mutation so paths can be copied only when a valid combination is found.
checklist: Implement both variants side by side and explain the changed next index.
Test duplicate candidates and an impossible target.
Prove that each output combination is generated once.

title: Reject conflicts before going deeper
subtitle: Grid paths and incremental constraint sets
why: Effective backtracking updates only the constraints affected by the new choice and rejects a conflict before exploring its descendants.
objectives: Track cells used by the current path.
Maintain column and diagonal conflicts incrementally.
Apply cheap feasibility checks before exponential search.

lesson.title: Path-local visitation
lesson.body: In a word search, a cell is unavailable only within the current attempted path. Mark it when entering and restore it when leaving so alternative starts and branches can use it.

lesson.title: One queen per row
lesson.body: Place queens row by row. Previously occupied columns and diagonals determine whether a candidate square is safe, eliminating the need to rescan the whole board.

lesson.title: Cheap rejection first
lesson.body: A word longer than the board or requiring more copies of a character than the board contains is impossible. Such necessary conditions avoid exploring a large search tree with no solution.

problems.title: Word Search
problems.brief: Determine whether a word can be formed by horizontal or vertical moves through a character grid, using each cell at most once in the path.
problems.target: O(rows·cols·4^L) simple upper bound, O(L) recursion space
hints: Try starts matching the first character.
At each step, inspect only adjacent matching unused cells.
Mark, recurse, and restore; precheck length and character counts.

problems.title: N-Queens
problems.brief: Return every arrangement of N queens on an N×N board with no shared row, column, or diagonal.
problems.target: Exponential search; O(N) constraint and recursion state excluding output
hints: Place exactly one queen in the current row.
Track used columns, row+col diagonals, and row-col diagonals.
Reject a conflicting square immediately and restore all three markers after recursion.

problems.title: Fox And Two Dots
problems.brief: In a grid of colored letters, determine whether four-directional movement forms a cycle of at least four distinct cells that all have the same color.
problems.target: O(rows·cols) time and O(rows·cols) traversal space.
hints: Start a DFS from each unvisited cell and follow only neighbors of the same color.
Carry the parent cell so the immediate reverse edge is ignored.
An edge to an already visited non-parent neighbor reveals an undirected cycle; a four-neighbor grid has no shorter simple cycle than four cells.

traps: Word-search visitation is local to a path, not global across the whole search.
A diagonal indexed by row-col requires a nonnegative offset.
Even an early successful return should respect the chosen input-restoration contract.

steps: Start at A in row 0, column 0.
Move right to B, marking both cells used for this path.
Move down from B to D.
All characters are matched without reusing a cell.

takeaway: Reject a conflict at the moment it is introduced, and restore every path-local constraint when backing out.
recall: Explain why one global visited set would miss valid word-search alternatives.
javaTip: Prefer boolean[] column and diagonal arrays for N-Queens; for grid marking, use a sentinel only if it cannot be a legal input character.
checklist: Test a word that would require reusing its first cell.
Explain both diagonal formulas.
Verify that the board remains unchanged after the method returns.

title: Prune symmetric assignments
subtitle: Equal-capacity buckets and subset-state thinking
why: Many expensive branches differ only in interchangeable bucket labels; recognizing that symmetry can remove most redundant exploration.
objectives: Reject impossible totals before assignment.
Try large items first to expose conflicts early.
Remove equivalent bucket choices without deleting distinct solutions.

lesson.title: Necessary arithmetic
lesson.body: Equal-sum partitioning requires a total divisible by the bucket count and no item larger than the target bucket sum. These checks reject impossible cases before recursion.

lesson.title: Fail early with large values
lesson.body: Sorting descending places the hardest-to-fit values first. This is an ordering heuristic rather than a proof of polynomial time, but it often reveals capacity conflicts near the root.

lesson.title: Buckets have no identity
lesson.body: If two buckets have the same current sum, placing the next value into either produces equivalent states up to bucket renaming. Try one representative, and stop after a failed placement into an empty bucket.

problems.title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
problems.brief: Partition positive integers into exactly K nonempty subsets with equal sums; each input index must be used once.
problems.target: Exponential worst case with symmetry and capacity pruning
hints: Check divisibility and maximum item against the target.
Sort descending and assign the next item to a bucket that stays within target.
Skip repeated bucket sums at one depth and symmetric empty buckets.

problems.title: Matchsticks to Square
problems.brief: Use every positive-length matchstick exactly once to form four sides of equal total length; sticks cannot be broken.
problems.target: Exponential worst case with four-bucket pruning
hints: The perimeter must be divisible by four.
Assign descending sticks to four side totals.
Treat equal current side totals as symmetric and reject capacity overflow immediately.

problems.title: Xenia and Weights
problems.brief: Choose m weights from the available values 1 through 10, placing them on alternating sides of a scale. Each move must make its side strictly heavier, and consecutive chosen weights must differ; output a valid sequence or NO.
problems.target: O(m·10³) time and O(m·10²) space with memoized states or DP and reconstruction.
hints: Let difference be the lead of the side used on the previous move, starting at zero.
A legal next weight w must be available, differ from the previous weight, and satisfy w>difference.
The new difference is w-difference; memoize (movesRemaining,lastWeight,difference) and retain choices to reconstruct an m-step sequence.

traps: Sorting improves search order but does not make the algorithm polynomial.
Symmetry pruning is valid only because buckets have identical rules.
A memo key containing only the next index is insufficient; partial assignments affect future feasibility.

steps: Total is 20, so each subset must sum to 5.
Place the largest item 5 alone.
Pair 4 with 1.
Pair each remaining 3 with one remaining 2.

takeaway: Prune interchangeable states only after proving that their labels do not affect any future rule.
recall: Give two calls with the same next index but different bucket sums and explain why their futures differ.
javaTip: For a small fixed bucket count, compare earlier bucket sums directly to skip symmetry instead of allocating a HashSet at every recursive call.
checklist: Test an indivisible total and one oversized item.
Explain the empty-bucket symmetry prune.
State a complete memoization key before attempting caching.

title: Recursion checkpoint: cache the right question
subtitle: Decision states, counting states, and the bridge to DP
why: The transition into dynamic programming begins by identifying recursive calls with identical future possibilities and caching their answers.
objectives: Define a complete memoization state.
Distinguish counting assignments from deciding existence.
Cache impossible and zero-answer states explicitly.

lesson.title: Same future, same question
lesson.body: For sign assignment, once the next index and current sum are known, earlier sign choices no longer affect the remaining possibilities. That pair is a reusable subproblem.

lesson.title: Count versus decide
lesson.body: Target Sum adds the number of completions from both choices. Equal partition combines choices with logical OR. Similar state graphs can require different aggregation and base cases.

lesson.title: Zero is an answer
lesson.body: A state with no completions is still computed work and must be cached. Use a separate uncomputed marker or map membership rather than treating zero or false as unvisited.

problems.title: Target Sum
problems.brief: Assign either + or - to every nonnegative integer and count assignments reaching the target; zeros still have two sign choices.
problems.target: O(n(S+1)) reachable-state bound with memoization, S=sum(nums)
hints: Use a state containing next index and current sum.
Branch by adding and subtracting the next value.
At the end return 1 only for the target sum; sum both branch counts and cache the result.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.brief: Decide whether positive integers can be divided into two subsets with equal sums, using every index exactly once; implement top-down memoization first.
problems.target: O(nS) time and memo space, S=half the total
hints: Reject an odd total.
Ask whether a subset of the remaining indices reaches total/2.
Memoize (index,remaining); combine skipping and taking the current value with OR.

problems.title: Cut Ribbon
problems.brief: Cut a ribbon of length n into pieces whose lengths are a, b, or c, using the entire ribbon. Maximize the number of pieces.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space for the three fixed cut lengths.
hints: Set dp[0]=0 and mark every other length unreachable.
For each total length, try appending each permitted cut to a reachable smaller length.
Maximize piece count rather than minimizing it; the answer must represent exactly n, not a shorter prefix.

traps: The two sign choices for zero count separately even though their next sums coincide.
Do not use one global visited set to replace a count of completions.
A false memo result must be distinguishable from an uncomputed state.

steps: Five positive signs produce sum 5.
Changing one sign from + to - reduces the sum by 2.
Exactly one negative sign is therefore required to reach 3.
Any of the five positions can be the negative one; memoization aggregates these distinct assignments.

takeaway: Memoization is correct when the key captures everything that can affect the remaining answer.
recall: Explain how the same recurrence can become a bottom-up table in the next phase without changing its meaning.
javaTip: Use Boolean[][] or a byte/int table with an explicit unknown marker for decision memoization; a boolean[][] alone cannot distinguish unknown from false.
checklist: Solve both from their recursive definitions before designing tables.
Test Target Sum with zeros and an unreachable target.
Write state, base case, transition, and aggregation in four sentences.

title: Turn recursion into a table
subtitle: Memoization, tabulation, and rolling states
why: You already know recursion; now make repeated subproblems explicit and choose a safe evaluation order.
objectives: Define a state in one sentence.
Translate a recurrence into bottom-up order.
Reduce memory only after identifying all dependencies.

lesson.title: Start with the choice
lesson.body: For House Robber, best(i) is the best sum from the first i houses. Either skip house i-1 or take it and use best(i-2).

lesson.title: Cache before compressing
lesson.body: Write the memoized version first, then fill a table from small prefixes to large prefixes. Both should evaluate the same states.

lesson.title: Keep the boundary visible
lesson.body: Use best(0)=0 for the empty house prefix. For digit decoding, the empty prefix has one decoding; a zero digit cannot decode alone, and two-digit choices must fall between 10 and 26.

problems.title: House Robber
problems.brief: For a nonnegative array, maximize the sum of selected values with no adjacent indices. Include empty input in your reusable method.
problems.target: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space after validating the table.
hints: Write take and skip choices for the last house.
best(i)=max(best(i-1), value[i-1]+best(i-2)).
Keep the previous two results; update using a temporary variable.

problems.title: Decode Ways
problems.brief: Count decodings of a nonempty digit string using 1→A through 26→Z. A zero is valid only inside 10 or 20.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space after validating the prefix table.
hints: Let dp[i] count decodings of the first i digits and set dp[0]=1.
If the last digit is nonzero, add dp[i-1].
If the last two digits form 10 through 26, also add dp[i-2].

problems.title: Boredom
problems.brief: Taking value x earns x points and removes remaining values x-1 and x+1. Aggregate repetitions and maximize the total.
problems.target: O(n+V) time and O(V) space, where V is the maximum value.
hints: Build points[x]=x*frequency[x].
Taking x forces skipping x-1; skipping x preserves the previous optimum.
Apply House Robber on the value axis and store totals in long.

traps: Do not overwrite a dependency before both transitions read it.
A zero digit is not a one-character decoding; test "0", "10", and "100" explicitly.
Be precise about whether a state includes the current element.

steps: best(0)=0; after house 2, best=2.

takeaway: A table is a recurrence evaluated in dependency order.
recall: Without notes, explain why a memoized state needs every input that can change its future answer.
javaTip: Keep rolling states in local variables; use long if n times the largest value can exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE.
checklist: Write both memoized and tabulated House Robber.
Verify empty and one-house inputs, then decoding cases "0", "10", and "226".
Explain the state before showing the loop.

title: Choose each item once
subtitle: Two-resource knapsack and balanced weight partitions
why: A subset state must track every limited resource; the same include-or-skip choice also turns stone smashing into balanced group sums.
objectives: Model two independent capacities.
Explain descending 0/1 updates.
Reduce stone smashing to a subset-sum difference.

lesson.title: Two capacities, one item
lesson.body: For Ones and Zeroes, dp[z][o] is the largest subset fitting both budgets. Count a string’s zeroes and ones before considering its inclusion.

lesson.title: Protect the previous-item layer
lesson.body: Update both capacities downward. An ascending update can reuse the current string, changing a 0/1 choice into unlimited reuse.

lesson.title: Balance the stone groups
lesson.body: Last Stone Weight II reduces to minimizing the difference between two subset sums. Find the largest reachable sum s<=total/2 and return total-2*s.

problems.title: Ones and Zeroes
problems.brief: Choose the largest subset of binary strings within budgets of m zeroes and n ones; each string is selected at most once and both budgets are at most 100.
problems.target: O(L+s*m*n) time and O(m*n) space, where L is total input length and s the string count.
hints: Count each string’s zeroes and ones.
Let dp[z][o] be the maximum subset size within both budgets.
Update both budgets downward to prevent reusing a string.

problems.title: Last Stone Weight II
problems.brief: Smash positive stones in pairs: equal weights disappear and unequal weights leave their difference. Minimize the final weight with at most 30 stones.
problems.target: O(nS) time and O(S) space, where S=floor(totalWeight/2).
hints: Represent the result as the difference between two group sums.
Find the largest achievable subset sum no greater than half the total.
Use descending 0/1 updates and return total-2*bestSubset.

problems.title: Red-Green Towers
problems.brief: Build a tallest tower with levels of 1,2,...,h blocks, each complete level red or green. Count maximum-height colorings under both supplies modulo 1,000,000,007.
problems.target: O(h*r) time and O(r) space, where h is the maximum height fitting r+g blocks.
hints: Find h with h*(h+1)/2<=r+g.
Red levels form a subset of level sizes; count sums using descending 0/1 updates.
Sum red usages for which both color supplies suffice.

traps: A string must fit both remaining budgets.
Descending only one budget does not generally prevent reuse.
The stone answer is total-2*bestSubset, not bestSubset itself.

steps: Taking "10" alone uses both budgets and selects one string.
Taking "0" uses the zero budget but leaves the one budget available.
Adding "1" gives two selected strings within both budgets.
All three strings exceed both budgets, so no larger subset is feasible.

takeaway: An item is used once even when its resource consumption has several dimensions.
recall: Compare this include-or-skip choice with House Robber; explain which constraints require today’s extra state dimensions.
javaTip: Count characters once per string, then update an int[m+1][n+1] table downward in both budget loops.
checklist: Trace a string that exceeds only one budget.
Implement both 0/1 reductions without copying a template.
Test repeated strings and an exactly balanced stone split.

title: Allow reuse without double-counting
subtitle: Unbounded knapsack and coin-change semantics
why: The same values produce different answers depending on whether you minimize coins, count combinations, or count ordered sequences.
objectives: Derive minimum-cost and counting transitions separately.
Use ascending amounts for unlimited reuse.
Distinguish combinations from permutations.

lesson.title: Minimum number of coins
lesson.body: Let dp[a] be the fewest coins needed for amount a. A final coin c gives dp[a-c]+1 when a>=c and the smaller amount is reachable.

lesson.title: Combination counting
lesson.body: For combinations, process each denomination outside and amounts inside. Once denomination c is processed, the table counts combinations using only denominations seen so far.

lesson.title: Observe a loop swap
lesson.body: If amount is outside and the last coin is inside, different orders can become different paths. Use amount 3 with coins 1 and 2 to expose the difference.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.brief: With distinct positive coin denominations available without limit, return the fewest coins for amount A, or -1 if impossible.
problems.target: O(kA) time and O(A) space.
hints: Initialize dp[0]=0 and other entries to an unreachable sentinel.
Try every coin as the final coin for each amount.
Only add one to a reachable previous state.

problems.title: Coin Change II
problems.brief: Count unordered combinations that make amount A using unlimited copies of distinct positive denominations.
problems.target: O(kA) time and O(A) space.
hints: There is one way to make zero: choose no coins.
Put the coin loop outside.
Update amounts from coin through A in ascending order.

problems.title: Flowers
problems.brief: For fixed k, count sequences of single red flowers and groups of k white flowers. Answer inclusive length-range count queries modulo 1,000,000,007.
problems.target: O(U+q) time and O(U) space, where U is the largest query endpoint.
hints: Start ways[0]=1.
The last choice contributes ways[x-1] or ways[x-k].
Prefix-sum these counts and subtract endpoints for each query.

traps: A zero-valued coin invalidates the usual recurrence.
Duplicate denominations can overcount if they are treated as distinct types.
For amount zero, the minimum is zero and the combination count is one.

steps: Start ways=[1,0,0,0].
After coin 1, ways=[1,1,1,1].
With coin 2, ways[2] becomes 2 and ways[3] becomes 2.
The combinations are 1+1+1 and 1+2; 2+1 is not a new combination.
dryRun.answer: 2 combinations; minimum number of coins is 2.

takeaway: Write what counts as a distinct answer before choosing loop order.
recall: Explain why yesterday’s 0/1 capacity loop descended while today’s unbounded loop ascends.
javaTip: Use an unreachable value such as A+1 for minimum coins when A is safely bounded; do not increment Integer.MAX_VALUE.
checklist: Trace both counting loop orders on amount 3.
Test amount zero and an unreachable amount.
State the denomination and counting assumptions aloud.

title: Track the best subsequence ending here
subtitle: LIS, binary-search tails, and counting optimal choices
why: Subsequence states depend on earlier compatible elements rather than one adjacent predecessor.
objectives: Define an ending-at-index state.
Explain what the tails array does and does not store.
Count optimal subsequences without discarding ties.

lesson.title: Quadratic baseline
lesson.body: For strictly increasing subsequences, len[i]=1+max(len[j]) over j<i with a[j]<a[i]. This is O(n²) and is the clearest correctness starting point.

lesson.title: Compress only the needed information
lesson.body: tails[t] stores the smallest possible ending value of an increasing subsequence of length t+1. Replace the first tail greater than or equal to the new value.

lesson.title: Count equal-quality predecessors
lesson.body: For counting, store both len[i] and count[i]. A better predecessor replaces the count; an equally good predecessor adds its count.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.brief: Return the length of a strictly increasing subsequence. Implement O(n²) first, then the tails method.
problems.target: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for the optimized length-only solution.
hints: Derive the ending-at-index DP first.
A smaller tail can serve every future extension that a larger tail can.
Find the first tails position with value >= current value.

problems.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.brief: Count index-distinct longest strictly increasing subsequences, including repeated input values.
problems.target: O(n²) time and O(n) space.
hints: Initialize every length and count to one.
Replace counts on a longer result and add counts on an equal-length result.
Sum counts only at indices with the global maximum length.

problems.title: Mysterious Present
problems.brief: Place a given card in an envelope chain with both dimensions strictly increasing. Return a longest chain with original envelope indices.
problems.target: O(n^2) time and O(n) DP space after sorting.
hints: Discard envelopes not strictly larger than the card in both dimensions.
Sort and run ending-at-envelope DP, checking both dimensions.
Store predecessor indices and reconstruct the chain.

traps: Strictly increasing uses <, not <=.
The final tails contents need not form a valid subsequence of the original array.
The length-only tails algorithm does not directly preserve the number of optimal subsequences.

steps: At 1: length 1, count 1.
At 3: length 2, count 1; at 5: length 3, count 1.
At 4: length 3, count 1.
At 7, both predecessors 5 and 4 give length 4, so their counts add.

takeaway: Optimize only after naming the information the answer still needs.
recall: Give one input where counting combinations and counting index-distinct subsequences differ.
javaTip: Implement lower-bound yourself for tails; Arrays.binarySearch does not promise which equal element it finds.
checklist: Compare both LIS methods on random small arrays.
Test equal values and descending order.
Explain both count replacement and count addition.

title: Move through grids with blocked states
subtitle: Path costs, path counts, and row compression
why: Grid DP makes dependency order visible and gives you a controlled setting for unreachable states.
objectives: Translate movement rules into dependencies.
Handle blocked start and destination cells.
Compress rows without mixing old and new meanings.

lesson.title: Acyclic movement
lesson.body: If moves are only right and down, each cell depends on its top and left neighbors. Row-major order evaluates both before the current cell.

lesson.title: Change the combine operator
lesson.body: For minimum cost, combine predecessors with min and add the cell cost. For path counting, add predecessor counts. The geometry is identical; the meaning is not.

lesson.title: Interpret one array carefully
lesson.body: Before updating dp[c], it still represents the cell above; dp[c-1] already represents the cell to the left. A blocked cell resets dp[c] to zero for counting.

problems.title: Minimum Path Sum
problems.brief: In a nonnegative rectangular grid, find the minimum sum from top-left to bottom-right using right and down moves.
problems.target: O(rows×cols) time and O(cols) auxiliary space.
hints: Include the current cell exactly once.
The first row and first column have only one possible predecessor.
Compress a table only after tracing the full version.

problems.title: Unique Paths II
problems.brief: Count right/down paths through a grid whose obstacle cells cannot be entered.
problems.target: O(rows×cols) time and O(cols) auxiliary space.
hints: A blocked cell contributes zero ways.
Seed the start with one only if it is open.
At each open cell, add ways from above and left.

problems.title: The least round way
problems.brief: Find a right/down grid path whose product has the fewest trailing decimal zeroes, and print it. Handle zero cells using the statement’s zero-product convention.
problems.target: O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space, including reconstruction.
hints: Count factors of two and five in each nonzero cell.
Run minimum-path DP separately for both factor counts.
If a zero exists and the best nonzero path costs more than one, route through zero with answer one.

traps: A blocked starting cell means zero paths immediately.
A cell cost is not the same thing as an obstacle flag.
Do not let an old value survive in the compressed array when a cell is blocked.

steps: After the first row, ways=[1,1,1].
On the middle row, the blocked center resets its count; ways=[1,0,1].
On the final row, propagate left and above to obtain [1,1,2].

takeaway: Compression is safe when you can name the meaning of every old and updated cell.
recall: State the difference between a path count and a minimum-cost state even when both use the same grid.
javaTip: Allocate columns+1 only if its extra boundary meaning is documented; off-by-one padding is not a substitute for base cases.
checklist: Trace a 1×1 grid and a blocked start.
Implement both problems with one row of storage.
Explain each compressed value before overwriting it.

title: Choose the state from the constraint
subtitle: Circular adjacency and value-based conflicts
why: Today checks whether you can recognize an earlier recurrence after the input format or boundary changes.
objectives: Reduce a circular constraint to linear cases.
Transform value conflicts into weighted positions.
Validate a reduction before reusing a template.

lesson.title: A boundary can split the problem
lesson.body: In a circular house arrangement, the first and last cannot both be selected. Solve the range excluding the first and the range excluding the last; take the larger result.

lesson.title: Group equivalent choices
lesson.body: In Delete and Earn, choosing a value removes its neighboring values. Aggregate equal values into total points, then solve the weighted adjacency problem.

lesson.title: Use a small brute-force oracle
lesson.body: For up to 15 items, enumerate subsets and check constraints directly. Compare your transformed DP to the oracle on small randomized inputs.

problems.title: House Robber II
problems.brief: Maximize a nonadjacent sum on a circular array of nonnegative house values.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Handle a single house before splitting ranges.
Every valid selection omits the first house or omits the last.
Call one linear helper on two index ranges without copying arrays.

problems.title: Delete and Earn
problems.brief: Earn x points by taking an occurrence of value x, which removes all occurrences of x-1 and x+1; maximize the total.
problems.target: O(n+V) time and O(V) space for bounded nonnegative values up to V.
hints: Combine all occurrences of a value into one weight.
Neighboring values conflict, even if they were far apart in the input.
Apply the take/skip recurrence across the value axis.

problems.title: Mortal Kombat Tower
problems.brief: You and a friend alternately defeat one or two consecutive bosses. Only the friend pays for hard bosses and the friend starts; minimize the payment.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space, reducible to constant rolling state.
hints: Use state (nextBoss,whoseTurn).
Try taking one boss and two bosses.
Charge hard bosses only on the friend’s turn, then switch turns.

traps: Running the linear robber algorithm once on the circle permits an illegal first-and-last selection.
With one house, the two-range reduction must not discard the only value.
A dense value array is wasteful when values are huge; sort unique values and account for gaps instead.

steps: Excluding the last gives [2,3], whose best sum is 3.
Excluding the first gives [3,2], whose best sum is 3.
Taking both 2s is illegal because they are adjacent around the circle.

takeaway: A familiar recurrence is useful only after the reduction preserves every constraint.
recall: From memory, contrast 0/1 updates, unbounded updates, and ending-at-index subsequence states.
javaTip: Pass inclusive or exclusive index ranges consistently to helpers; avoid Arrays.copyOfRange just to simplify loop bounds.
checklist: Solve both problems from a blank Java file.
Compare against subset enumeration for small inputs.
Write one sentence explaining why each reduction is valid.

title: Align two sequences
subtitle: LCS and counting matching subsequences
why: Two-index states model progress through two sequences and lead directly to many string DP problems.
objectives: Explain a state over two prefixes.
Separate choosing an optimum from counting all choices.
Handle empty-prefix base cases.

lesson.title: LCS prefix state
lesson.body: dp[i][j] is the LCS length for the first i and j characters. Equal final characters can extend the diagonal; otherwise skip one final character.

lesson.title: Count embeddings
lesson.body: For Distinct Subsequences, dp[i][j] counts ways the first i source characters form the first j target characters. A matching source character may be used or skipped.

lesson.title: Make empty prefixes explicit
lesson.body: Any source prefix forms the empty target in one way. An empty source forms a nonempty target in zero ways. These bases carry through the whole counting table.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.brief: Return the length of a longest common subsequence of two strings; characters need not be contiguous.
problems.target: O(nm) time; O(min(n,m)) space for length-only row compression.
hints: Draw a table with one extra row and column.
On equal characters, extend the diagonal by one.
Otherwise take the maximum of skipping from either string.

problems.title: Distinct Subsequences
problems.brief: Count the ways to delete source characters so the remaining sequence equals the target. Equal characters at different source indices give different choices.
problems.target: O(nm) time and O(m) space; use an appropriate count type for the stated bounds.
hints: You may always skip the current source character.
If it matches, also count ways that use it as the current target character.
For one-dimensional storage, update target positions in descending order.

problems.title: Hard problem
problems.brief: Keep strings in original order but optionally reverse each at its cost, making the sequence lexicographically nondecreasing. Return minimum cost or -1.
problems.target: O(L) overall comparison work and preprocessing, where L is total string length; O(L) string storage and O(1) rolling DP states.
hints: Each string has original and reversed forms.
Keep the cheapest prefix ending in each form.
Check all previous/current form pairs and guard unreachable costs.

traps: LCS is a subsequence problem, not longest common substring.
Do not initialize all counting cells to one; only the empty-target column has that meaning.
Ascending target updates reuse a source character more than once.

steps: The r and a must come from their matching source positions.
The target needs two b characters from three source b positions.
There are three ways to choose those two positions; i and t are then fixed.

takeaway: The table shape does not determine whether transitions use max, min, or addition.
recall: Explain why one-dimensional 0/1 subset DP and one-dimensional Distinct Subsequences both update backward.
javaTip: For unrestricted counts use BigInteger; for a bounded challenge, document the guaranteed result range before selecting int or long.
checklist: Implement both full tables before compressing.
Test an empty target and disjoint alphabets.
Say whether your state counts choices or stores an optimum.

title: Model edits and wildcard consumption
subtitle: String transitions with different meanings
why: Edit costs and pattern symbols change how many characters a transition consumes; writing that explicitly prevents memorized-but-wrong recurrences.
objectives: Map each edit to a predecessor state.
Explain both interpretations of wildcard *.
Initialize pattern-only and text-only boundaries.

lesson.title: Edit distance
lesson.body: To transform one prefix into another, the final step is an insertion, deletion, or replacement. Equal final characters can keep the diagonal cost unchanged.

lesson.title: Wildcard matching
lesson.body: For wildcard matching, ? consumes exactly one character and * consumes zero or more. A star either disappears or consumes a text character while remaining available.

lesson.title: Meaning before notation
lesson.body: State which index is text and which is pattern. This makes the zero-character star transition and empty-text row unambiguous.

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.brief: Find the minimum number of unit-cost insertions, deletions, and replacements needed to transform one string into another.
problems.target: O(nm) time and O(min(n,m)) auxiliary space after row compression.
hints: Use dp[i][0]=i and dp[0][j]=j.
Match equal characters for free.
Otherwise add one to the minimum insertion, deletion, or replacement predecessor.

problems.title: Wildcard Matching
problems.brief: Match a whole string against a pattern containing lowercase characters, ? and *. Here * is an independent wildcard, not a regex repetition operator.
problems.target: O(nm) time and O(m) space with two rows.
hints: Initialize the empty-text row from leading stars only.
A literal or ? consumes one character from both sides.
For *, combine zero consumed characters with at least one consumed character.

problems.title: Caesar's Legions
problems.brief: Arrange n1 footmen and n2 horsemen with runs no longer than k1 and k2. Count valid arrangements modulo 100,000,000.
problems.target: O(n1*n2*(k1+k2)) time and O(n1*n2) space with last-block states.
hints: Track both used counts and the final block’s type.
Append an opposite-type block within its run limit.
Initialize single-type arrangements explicitly so an empty start is not counted twice.

traps: Wildcard matching and regular-expression matching have different * semantics.
A pattern such as "**a" does not match empty text.
During row compression, diagonal, above, and left values must retain their intended rows.

steps: Replace h with r: "rorse".
Delete the extra r after o: "rose".
Delete e: "ros".
The edit-distance table gives minimum cost 3.

takeaway: For every transition, say which characters it consumes and what it costs.
recall: Rebuild the LCS mismatch transition and explain why Edit Distance must consider a diagonal replacement too.
javaTip: Use charAt(i-1) only for states with i>0; keeping the empty-prefix row prevents negative-index special cases.
checklist: Trace the three edit operations on a tiny pair.
Test empty strings and a pattern made entirely of stars.
Explain why the wildcard star recurrence has two branches.

title: Pay for the final partition
subtitle: Palindrome cost tables and exact-part counts
why: Precomputing a segment property turns expensive repeated string work into constant-time transitions.
objectives: Precompute palindrome information by interval length.
Distinguish minimum cuts from exactly K parts.
Keep impossible partition counts unreachable.

lesson.title: Segment preprocessing
lesson.body: For a palindrome check, compare the ends and reuse the inner interval. For replacement cost, add one when the ends differ and continue inward.

lesson.title: Minimum cuts
lesson.body: Choose the start of the final palindromic segment. Everything before that segment is a shorter prefix whose optimal answer is already known.

lesson.title: Exactly K parts
lesson.body: Let dp[p][i] be the minimum replacement cost to split the first i characters into exactly p nonempty parts. Try the final split point j and add cost[j][i-1].

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning II
problems.brief: Split a string into palindromic substrings and return the minimum number of cuts.
problems.target: O(n²) time and O(n²) space with a precomputed palindrome table.
hints: Precompute whether each interval is a palindrome.
A prefix that is already a palindrome needs zero cuts.
Otherwise try every valid final palindromic segment.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning III
problems.brief: Change as few characters as possible so a string can be split into exactly K nonempty palindromic substrings; assume 1<=K<=n.
problems.target: O(n²+Kn²) time and O(n²+Kn) space.
hints: Compute mismatch-pair cost for every interval.
Start only dp[0][0]=0; other zero-part states are impossible.
For p parts, use split positions that leave every part nonempty.

problems.title: Zuma
problems.brief: Remove a contiguous palindromic block of marbles in one move; remaining marbles close the gap. Minimize moves to remove everything.
problems.target: O(n^3) time and O(n^2) interval-DP space.
hints: Let dp[l][r] be the minimum moves for an interval.
Baseline: remove a[l] alone and solve [l+1,r].
For a[l]==a[k], clear the interior and absorb equal ends into its last removal; adjacent equal ends take one move, then add the suffix cost.

traps: K parts require K-1 cuts, so the two answer conventions differ.
For exact K parts, a zero-filled table incorrectly marks impossible states reachable.
An interval with equal ends still needs its inner interval checked.

steps: Split as "a" | "bc": the single character costs 0 and "bc" costs 1 replacement.
Split as "ab" | "c": the costs are 1 and 0.
Both legal splits cost 1; no two-part split costs 0.

takeaway: Choose the final segment, then solve the remaining prefix with one fewer part.
recall: Write the edit-distance base row, then explain why exact-partition DP needs infinity rather than ordinary edit counts.
javaTip: Use a large finite INF such as 1_000_000_000 when n bounds the true cost; guard unreachable predecessors before addition.
checklist: Build and inspect the segment-cost table for "abcba".
Test K=1 and K=n.
Explain why split bounds enforce nonempty parts.

title: Add length constraints to segment DP
subtitle: Minimum segment length and bounded block choices
why: Partition constraints often hide an optimization: a moving set of eligible split points can replace an inner scan.
objectives: Model exactly K nonoverlapping segments.
Derive a prefix-sum transition.
Maintain the best eligible split value safely.

lesson.title: Separate selection from coverage
lesson.body: Exactly K subarrays need not cover the entire array. Define dp[k][i] as the best sum of k valid subarrays inside the first i positions, allowing skipped positions.

lesson.title: Rearrange a transition
lesson.body: If the final subarray is [j,i), its sum is prefix[i]-prefix[j]. For minimum length M, j<=i-M, so maintain max(dp[k-1][j]-prefix[j]) over eligible j.

lesson.title: Bounded blocks
lesson.body: For Partition Array for Maximum Sum, every element is covered and a block has length at most K. Scan up to K previous positions while maintaining the block maximum.

problems.title: Sum of K Subarrays With Length at Least M
problems.brief: Maximize the sum of exactly k nonoverlapping subarrays of length at least m. Values may be negative; n<=2000, 1<=m<=3, and k*m<=n.
problems.target: O(nk) time and O(n) rolling-row space.
hints: Let dp[t][i] mean the best t selections in the first i positions.
For endpoint i, maintain max(dp[t-1][j]-prefix[j]) over j<=i-m.
Also allow skipping position i; unreachable positive-selection states need negative infinity.

problems.title: Partition Array for Maximum Sum
problems.brief: Partition the entire array into blocks of at most K elements; replace every element of a block by its maximum and maximize the total.
problems.target: O(nK) time and O(n) space.
hints: Try every legal length for the final block.
Extend backward while updating the block maximum.
Candidate=best[prefixBeforeBlock]+length×blockMaximum.

problems.title: George and Job
problems.brief: Select exactly k disjoint length-m subarrays of a positive array to maximize their sum. Gaps are allowed.
problems.target: O(nk) time and O(n) rolling-row space.
hints: Compute fixed-window sums with prefix sums.
At each prefix, skip its last position or take the window ending there.
Taking reads the previous selection layer at i-m.

traps: Exactly K selections can require a negative answer; initializing all states to zero changes the problem.
Reject K×M>n before optimization.
Minimum-length selection allows gaps, while full-array partitioning does not.

steps: The first length-two subarray [1,2] has sum 3.
The disjoint final subarray [4,3] has sum 7.
Skipping -5 is allowed because the task selects subarrays rather than covering the whole array.
Any extension that includes -5 reduces the selected total.

takeaway: Algebra can reveal which part of a transition should be maintained incrementally.
recall: Contrast exactly K parts covering a string with exactly K selected subarrays that may leave gaps.
javaTip: Use long prefix sums and a safe NEG_INF; never add a prefix to an impossible state.
checklist: Derive the O(Kn²) recurrence before optimizing it.
Compare optimized and brute-force results on short arrays.
Test all-negative values and the tight case K×M=n.

title: Encode completed choices with a mask
subtitle: Assignment and capacity-packed work sessions
why: When the number of items is small, a subset can be an exact state instead of a complicated collection of flags.
objectives: Define each bit and estimate 2^N states before coding.
Infer a worker index from bit count.
Compare compound DP results lexicographically.

lesson.title: A subset is a state
lesson.body: For N<=20, a mask can record assigned jobs. If workers are assigned in a fixed order, bitCount(mask) identifies the next worker, so it need not be another dimension.

lesson.title: Transitions add one choice
lesson.body: For every unassigned job j, relax mask|(1<<j) with the cost for the next worker. Each transition increases bit count, giving a natural evaluation order.

lesson.title: Keep the strongest partial packing
lesson.body: For work sessions, retain the pair with fewer sessions; among equal session counts, prefer less load in the last session. Every task must fit in an empty session.

problems.title: Minimum XOR Sum of Two Arrays
problems.brief: Permute the second array to minimize the sum of pairwise XOR values. Both arrays have equal length at most 14.
problems.target: O(n*2^n) time and O(2^n) space.
hints: Mask assigned positions in the second array.
Integer.bitCount(mask) gives the next first-array position.
Try every unused second-array index and add that pair’s XOR cost.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Work Sessions to Finish the Tasks
problems.brief: Pack positive task durations into the fewest sessions of fixed capacity. Tasks cannot be split; every task fits individually and N<=14.
problems.target: O(N2^N) time and O(2^N) space using (sessionCount,lastLoad) per mask.
hints: For a nonempty task set, initialize the empty mask with one empty session.
Append a task to the current session when it fits; otherwise open a new one.
Prefer fewer sessions, then a smaller current-session load.

problems.title: Kefa and Dishes
problems.brief: Choose and order exactly m of n dishes to maximize base satisfaction plus directed consecutive-pair bonuses. n<=18.
problems.target: O(n^2*2^n) time and O(n*2^n) space.
hints: Use (mask,last), since the next bonus depends on the endpoint.
Initialize one-dish states with their base satisfaction.
Append unused dishes with their value and pair bonus; answer only masks of size m.

traps: Bitmask DP is impractical when N is large even if each transition is simple.
Use 1<<N only within the chosen int-mask range.
For assignment, an unreachable mask must not contribute a seemingly cheap default cost.

steps: At mask 00, worker 0 may take job 0 for 9 or job 1 for 2.
After choosing job 0, worker 1 must take job 1: total 9+4=13.
After choosing job 1, worker 1 must take job 0: total 2+6=8.
dryRun.answer: 8: worker 0 takes job 1; worker 1 takes job 0.

takeaway: A dimension can disappear when the rest of the state determines it.
recall: Explain how today’s mask differs from yesterday’s numeric capacity: one records identities, the other records an amount.
javaTip: Use primitive arrays for mask costs and pair components; hundreds of thousands of small Java objects add avoidable memory overhead.
checklist: Estimate the state and transition counts for N=20.
Compare assignment DP against permutation enumeration for N<=8.
Test work sessions with one task and with every task filling a session.

title: Choose what a subset state remembers
subtitle: Coverage masks and shortest-superstring endpoints
why: A coverage problem and an ordering problem both use masks, but only ordering needs the previous endpoint to price the next choice.
objectives: Separate coverage from one-to-one assignment.
Explain when a last-item dimension is necessary.
Reconstruct a shortest-superstring ordering.

lesson.title: Cover every point
lesson.body: For Connect Two Groups, process first-group points and mask covered second-group points. Give every first-group point one connection; multiple points may choose the same neighbor.

lesson.title: Finish uncovered points
lesson.body: After processing the first group, connect every missing second-group point by its cheapest incident edge. Compare this completion cost for every final mask. There is no one-connection-per-point restriction.

lesson.title: Keep an endpoint for overlaps
lesson.body: For Shortest Superstring, appending j after i costs length(j)-overlap(i,j). Use dp[mask][last], store predecessor states, and reconstruct the order before appending nonoverlapping suffixes.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Connect Two Groups of Points
problems.brief: Connect two groups so each point has at least one connection, minimizing nonnegative cost. The smaller group has at most 12 points; multiple connections are allowed.
problems.target: O(m*n*2^n) time and O(2^n) rolling space, where n is the smaller group size.
hints: Mask covered points in the second group.
Process each first-group point and give it one connection.
For every final mask, cover missing second-group points at their cheapest incident cost.

problems.title: Find the Shortest Superstring
problems.brief: Find a shortest string containing every input string. After removing contained strings, use pairwise suffix-prefix overlaps to choose an order; any shortest answer is acceptable.
problems.target: O(N²2^N+N²L²) time with naive overlap preprocessing; O(N2^N+N²) DP/preprocessing space, excluding output.
hints: Precompute how much of the next string is already covered by the current suffix.
Use dp[mask][last] for the minimum constructed length.
Store the previous endpoint and reconstruct before appending only nonoverlapping suffixes.

problems.title: Roman and Numbers
problems.brief: Count distinct digit permutations divisible by m, excluding leading zeroes. At most 18 digits and m<=100 make subset-and-remainder DP possible.
problems.target: O(2^n*n*m) time and O(2^n*m) space; estimate memory before allocation.
hints: Use (usedDigitMask,currentRemainder).
Appending d gives (remainder*10+d)%m; forbid a first zero.
Sort digits and skip an equal occurrence unless the previous equal occurrence is already used.

traps: Connect Two Groups permits multiple connections per point.
Bit count does not identify how many first-group rows were processed when several rows chose the same neighbor.
Shortest-superstring overlaps can be asymmetric; containment must be handled if the input does not rule it out.

steps: Connect first-group point 0 to second-group point 0 for cost 1.
Connect first-group points 1 and 2 to second-group point 2 for total cost 2.
Second-group point 1 remains uncovered; its cheapest connection costs 1 from first-group point 0.
The completed solution uses four cost-one edges and covers every point.
dryRun.answer: 4. The optimal solution is not a one-to-one matching.

takeaway: A mask records selected identities; keep an endpoint only when it changes the next transition.
recall: Explain why assignment inferred the worker from bit count, but today’s coverage DP must process first-group rows separately.
javaTip: Use rolling long[] or int[] rows for coverage masks; use a parent table only for the superstring reconstruction that needs an order.
checklist: Trace a solution that connects one point more than once.
Explain why missing-point completion is valid with nonnegative costs.
Reconstruct a superstring and verify it contains every input.

title: Give every traversal a purpose
subtitle: Level order, DFS paths, and recursive return values
why: Tree work becomes easier when you separate information traveling down a path from information returning up from children.
objectives: Choose BFS for levels and DFS for root-to-leaf paths.
Keep path mutation local to a recursion branch.
Express complexity including returned output.

lesson.title: Breadth first means one level at a time
lesson.body: Record the queue size before processing a level. Nodes appended during that loop belong to the next level.

lesson.title: Depth first carries path context
lesson.body: For root-to-leaf path sums, carry a running sum and a mutable path. Only leaves can finish an answer; a matching internal prefix is not sufficient.

lesson.title: Backtrack the path
lesson.body: Append a node before exploring its children and remove it afterward. Copy the path only when storing an answer, otherwise all answers may share one changing list.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.brief: Return the values grouped by depth from left to right. Handle an empty tree.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(w) auxiliary queue space, where w is maximum width; O(n) output.
hints: Use a queue of nodes.
Freeze the queue size at the start of each level.
Append children while processing that fixed number of nodes.

problems.title: Path Sum II
problems.brief: Return every root-to-leaf path whose node values sum to target; values may be negative.
problems.target: O(n+L) time, where L is total output length; O(h) auxiliary DFS/path space, excluding output.
hints: Carry the current path and remaining target.
Check the sum only when both children are absent.
Copy the successful path, then remove its last element during backtracking.

problems.title: Kefa and Park
problems.brief: Count root-to-leaf restaurant paths in a tree with no more than m consecutive cat vertices.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) worst-case traversal space.
hints: Carry the consecutive-cat count down the DFS.
Reset it at cat-free vertices and prune above m.
Count only leaves whose entire root path remained valid.

traps: Negative values make a simple running-sum-greater-than-target prune invalid.
The root alone is a valid root-to-leaf path only when it is a leaf.
A degenerate tree can have recursion depth n and overflow the Java stack.

steps: The queue starts with root 3, producing level [3].
Its children 9 and 20 produce level [9,20].
Only 20 has children, producing level [15,7].

takeaway: Choose traversal order from the information the answer needs.
recall: Explain the difference between DFS path state and a memoized DP state that is reused across branches.
javaTip: Use ArrayDeque<TreeNode>; it does not accept null, so enqueue only existing children.
checklist: Implement both BFS and path DFS.
Test empty, single-node, and chain-shaped trees.
Show why stored paths need copies.

title: Use the full BST invariant
subtitle: Ancestor bounds and ordered selection
why: A binary-search tree is constrained by all ancestors, which gives both a validation method and an ordered traversal.
objectives: Validate a node against inherited bounds.
Use inorder order for kth selection.
Distinguish node identity from its value.

lesson.title: Bounds come from ancestors
lesson.body: For a strict BST, every value in the left subtree must be smaller than the node and every value in the right subtree larger. Checking only direct children is insufficient.

lesson.title: Inorder is globally sorted
lesson.body: Left, node, right visits strict-BST keys in increasing order. The kth visit gives the kth smallest key without sorting a separate collection.

lesson.title: Choose early stopping
lesson.body: An iterative inorder traversal can stop at the kth node. Its cost is O(h+k), and its explicit stack is at most the tree height.

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.brief: Check whether a binary tree is a strict BST with no duplicate keys, including nodes at the int limits.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(h) auxiliary space.
hints: Pass an allowed open interval to each node.
The left subtree inherits a new upper bound; the right inherits a new lower bound.
Use long bounds or nullable bounds so int extremes remain valid.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problems.brief: Given a strict BST and 1<=k<=number of nodes, return its kth smallest value.
problems.target: O(h+k) time and O(h) space with early-stopping iterative inorder.
hints: Push the entire left spine.
Pop one node and decrement k.
Then process the right child’s left spine.

problems.title: Christmas Spruce
problems.brief: Check that every internal vertex of a rooted tree has at least three immediate children that are leaves.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space.
hints: Build child counts from the parent list.
A rooted leaf has zero children.
Count immediate leaf children for each internal vertex and reject fewer than three.

traps: A right child of a left-subtree node may still violate the root’s bound.
Using Integer.MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE as exclusive bounds rejects valid extreme keys.
The method relies on an agreed duplicate-key convention.

steps: Push 5, then 3, then 2 onto the inorder stack.
Visit 2 first and 3 second.
The right subtree of 3 yields 4 as the third visit.

takeaway: The BST property applies to whole subtrees, not just neighboring nodes.
recall: Describe why level order cannot directly identify the kth smallest BST value.
javaTip: Use long lower and upper bounds, or compare using nullable Integer bounds; do not use subtraction for ordering.
checklist: Reject the invalid tree [5,1,6,null,null,3,7].
Test an int-minimum key in a one-node BST.
Explain the O(h+k) early-stop bound.

title: Find where two paths meet
subtitle: Lowest common ancestors in ordinary trees and BSTs
why: The same question has different efficient solutions depending on whether key ordering is available.
objectives: Define the information returned by an LCA recursion.
Handle the case where one target is an ancestor.
Use BST ordering only when guaranteed.

lesson.title: Ordinary-tree return contract
lesson.body: Return null if neither target is found below a node, a target if only that target is found, or the LCA if both are found. If both child calls return non-null, the current node is the split.

lesson.title: A target can be the ancestor
lesson.body: When the current node is one of the targets, return it immediately under the standard assumption that both targets exist in the tree.

lesson.title: BST descent
lesson.body: In a BST, if both targets are smaller, go left; if both are larger, go right. Otherwise the current node is the split or one target itself.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
problems.brief: Given node references p and q that both exist, return their lowest common ancestor. Do not rely on key ordering.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(h) auxiliary recursion space.
hints: Return a target node when you encounter it.
Recurse into both children.
Two non-null child results make the current node the answer.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
problems.brief: Given a strict BST and two existing target nodes, find their LCA using ordering.
problems.target: O(h) time and O(1) auxiliary space with iterative descent.
hints: Compare both target values with the current key.
Descend only when both lie on the same side.
Stop when they split or one equals the current node.

problems.title: Tree Queries
problems.brief: For each query set, decide whether its vertices all lie on or within one edge of some path beginning at the tree root.
problems.target: O(n+sum(querySizes)) time and O(n) space with depth and DFS intervals.
hints: Replace queried vertices by their parents, keeping the root unchanged.
Choose the deepest original queried vertex as a candidate path endpoint.
Each replaced vertex must be its ancestor; test DFS entry/exit intervals.

traps: If targets may be missing, the standard ordinary-tree solution needs additional presence checks.
Compare references for ordinary-tree targets when values may repeat.
The BST shortcut is invalid on a general binary tree.

steps: The recursion reaches node 5 and returns that target reference.
Node 4 lies inside node 5’s subtree.
No lower descendant of 5 can be an ancestor of node 5 itself.

takeaway: Write the recursive return contract before writing the two child calls.
recall: Explain how ancestor bounds from BST validation justify choosing only one LCA branch.
javaTip: Compare TreeNode references with == when the input supplies target nodes; value equality may identify a different node.
checklist: Test targets in opposite subtrees.
Test one target being the ancestor of the other.
State whether missing targets are allowed.

title: Separate the returned branch from the global path
subtitle: Diameter and maximum path sum
why: A path may join two child branches at one node, but only one branch can continue upward to the parent.
objectives: Define a one-branch return value.
Evaluate a through-node candidate separately.
Handle negative values and edge-count conventions.

lesson.title: One branch travels upward
lesson.body: For a parent to extend a path through its child, that child can return only its best single downward branch. Returning both branches would create a fork.

lesson.title: Two branches may finish here
lesson.body: At a node, the longest or highest-value finished path can combine left and right branches. Update a global optimum with this through-node candidate.

lesson.title: Different bases for different questions
lesson.body: Diameter usually counts edges, while heights may count nodes. Maximum path sum requires a nonempty path, so the global answer must allow negative values.

problems.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
problems.brief: Return the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. Implement both recursive and iterative-postorder versions for depth stress.
problems.target: O(n) time; O(h) recursion space, or O(n) for a straightforward explicit-postorder implementation.
hints: Let an empty subtree have height zero and a leaf height one.
The diameter candidate through a node is leftHeight+rightHeight.
Return 1+max(leftHeight,rightHeight).

problems.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.brief: Return the maximum sum of a nonempty simple path; the path may start and end anywhere and node values may be negative.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(h) auxiliary recursion space.
hints: Discard a negative child contribution by replacing it with zero.
Update the answer with nodeValue+leftGain+rightGain.
Return nodeValue+max(leftGain,rightGain) to the parent.

problems.title: Tree Painting
problems.brief: Choose the first vertex maximizing tree-painting score. For a fixed root, the score equals the sum of subtree sizes, or n plus the sum of depths.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space using rerooting.
hints: Compute subtree sizes and an initial depth sum.
Across u→v, sub[v] vertices move one step closer and all others farther.
Use score[v]=score[u]+n-2*sub[v] and maximize.

traps: An all-negative tree must return its largest node value, not zero.
The best path need not pass through the root.
Do not return the sum of both branches to a parent.

steps: Node 20 receives gains 15 and 7.
Its through-node path sums to 15+20+7=42.
It returns only 20+max(15,7)=35 upward.
The root candidate is -10+9+35=34, so 42 remains best.

takeaway: The value returned to a parent can differ from the answer completed at the current node.
recall: Describe the LCA split point, then relate it to a path that joins two child branches.
javaTip: Reset per-call answer fields before each public invocation; stale object fields can corrupt repeated tests.
checklist: Trace an all-negative tree.
State whether diameter is measured in edges or nodes.
Stress a long chain with an explicit stack version.

title: Let the parent see a small set of choices
subtitle: Independent-set DP and camera coverage states
why: Tree DP summarizes a subtree by the decisions that matter at its boundary with the parent.
objectives: Derive take/skip states for adjacency conflicts.
Design coverage states for cameras.
Explain why child subproblems become independent after fixing the parent state.

lesson.title: Take or skip the current node
lesson.body: For a weighted independent set, taking u forces every child to be skipped. Skipping u allows each child to choose its better state.

lesson.title: Coverage needs more than a boolean
lesson.body: For cameras, distinguish: has a camera, covered without a camera, and not yet covered. Each state changes what the parent must provide.

lesson.title: Make null children harmless
lesson.body: In a camera-state implementation, null children need no camera and should not force one. At the root, an uncovered state must be resolved because there is no parent.

problems.title: House Robber III
problems.brief: Maximize selected nonnegative node values in a binary tree without selecting both endpoints of a parent-child edge.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(h) auxiliary recursion space.
hints: Return two values from each node: take and skip.
take=nodeValue+leftSkip+rightSkip.
skip=max(leftTake,leftSkip)+max(rightTake,rightSkip).

problems.title: Binary Tree Cameras
problems.brief: Place the fewest cameras so every node is covered by a camera on itself, its parent, or a child.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(h) auxiliary recursion space.
hints: Process children before deciding the parent.
If a child is uncovered, the current node must receive a camera in the greedy three-state formulation.
If the root remains uncovered, add one final camera.

problems.title: Uncle Bogdan and Country Happiness
problems.brief: Check whether good/bad moods can satisfy the stated populations and happiness values throughout a tree.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space per test case.
hints: Compute every subtree’s population s in postorder.
Its good count (s+h)/2 must be integral and in [0,s].
good[u]-sum(good[child]) must lie between zero and the local population at u.

traps: Tree independent set forbids parent-child pairs, not nodes at the same depth.
A covered node and a node with a camera are different states.
For cameras, returning an uncovered root without fixing it undercounts.

steps: The leaf values 3 and 1 each return take=value and skip=0.
The left child 2 has take=2 and skip=3; the right child 3 has take=3 and skip=1.
At the root, take=3+3+1=7 and skip=max(2,3)+max(3,1)=6.
dryRun.answer: 7, selecting the root and the two grandchildren.

takeaway: A good tree state tells the parent what it may choose and what it must supply.
recall: Connect House Robber on an array to House Robber on a tree by describing the changed dependency structure.
javaTip: A small result record or two-element array is clear for interviews; for very large trees, measure allocation overhead or use indexed primitive tables.
checklist: Derive the take and skip equations without notes.
Trace cameras on a one-node tree and a three-node chain.
Explain the root-specific camera correction.

title: Combine a tree with a resource budget
subtitle: Distance frontiers and parent-dependent stock discounts
why: A tree’s parent relation can be a movement edge or information that changes a child’s price; model the role required by each problem.
objectives: Search distances using parent links.
Track whether a parent purchased stock.
Merge child budgets without exceeding the initial budget.

lesson.title: Distance can move upward
lesson.body: For Distance K, build parent links and run BFS from the target through parent, left, and right neighbors. Mark visited nodes so the search cannot immediately walk back.

lesson.title: A parent decision changes price
lesson.body: For stock discounts, the state contains the subtree budget and whether the direct parent bought stock. Buying the current employee sets the discount flag for its children.

lesson.title: Merge spending, not future earnings
lesson.body: Combine child budget tables with knapsack merges, then compare buying and skipping the current stock. All purchases must fit the initial budget; future profit cannot fund another purchase.

problems.title: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree
problems.brief: Return all nodes exactly K edges from a given target node that exists in the tree; output order is arbitrary.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.
hints: Build a map from each node to its parent.
Run BFS from the target using left, right, and parent neighbors.
After K levels, return the current frontier.

problems.title: Maximum Profit from Trading Stocks with Discounts
problems.brief: Choose stocks in an employee tree within an initial budget. Buying a direct manager’s stock halves an employee’s price; tomorrow’s profit cannot fund purchases. n and budget are at most 160.
problems.target: O(n*budget^2) time and O(n*budget) DP space.
hints: Keep subtree budget tables for each parent-bought flag.
Compare skipping an employee against buying at its flag-dependent price.
Merge child budgets; buying the current employee gives discounts only to direct children.

problems.title: Distance in Tree
problems.brief: Count unordered pairs of distinct tree vertices at exactly distance k, with n<=50,000 and k<=500.
problems.target: O(nk) time and O(nk) space; use long for the pair count.
hints: Store cnt[u][d] for already processed subtree vertices at distance d from u.
Before merging a child, add cnt[u][d]*cnt[child][k-d-1].
Then shift child distances by one into u; querying first prevents same-child double-counting.

traps: Distance K counts edges; K=0 returns the target.
A locally unprofitable manager may unlock profitable child discounts.
Discounts depend on the direct manager, and tomorrow’s sale revenue cannot increase today’s budget.

steps: Buying employee 1 costs 1 and earns profit 2-1=1.
Because the direct manager bought stock, employee 2 costs floor(4/2)=2.
Buying both spends 3 and earns profit 1+(6-2)=5.
Employee 2 alone costs 4 and is unaffordable; employee 1 alone earns only 1.

takeaway: The subtree state must expose both the resource used and the parent choice affecting its transitions.
recall: Compare the two take/skip values in House Robber III with today’s budget table and parent-bought flag.
javaTip: Use fresh destination arrays when merging child budgets so one child cannot be reused; keep unreachable spending states explicit.
checklist: Solve Distance K with parent links and a visited set.
Trace buying a manager to unlock its child’s discount.
Test zero budget and a stock whose own profit is negative.

title: Choose traversal from edge meaning
subtitle: Components and unweighted shortest paths
why: Trees had one route between nodes; graphs can revisit vertices, so discovery and distance rules now matter.
objectives: Mark vertices at discovery to prevent repeated work.
Use BFS only when each traversed edge has equal cost.
Translate a grid into neighbors with the stated movement rules.

lesson.title: Components need reachability
lesson.body: For island counting, start a traversal from each unvisited land cell. One complete traversal marks exactly one connected component.

lesson.title: BFS gives distance layers
lesson.body: With unit-cost edges, the first discovery of a vertex gives its shortest distance. Mark it when enqueuing so several parents do not enqueue it repeatedly.

lesson.title: The neighbor rule is part of the problem
lesson.body: Number of Islands uses four directions; Shortest Path in Binary Matrix uses eight. Neither rule should be guessed from a remembered grid template.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.brief: Count four-direction-connected groups of land in a rectangular grid. Decide whether your method may mutate the grid.
problems.target: O(rows×cols) time and O(rows×cols) worst-case traversal storage.
hints: Scan every cell, starting a traversal only on unvisited land.
Mark a cell before adding its neighbors.
Each new traversal increases the component count once.

problems.title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
problems.brief: In a square binary grid, move through open cells in eight directions; return the shortest path length in visited cells, or -1.
problems.target: O(n²) time and O(n²) space.
hints: Reject a blocked start or destination.
Start BFS distance at one because the starting cell counts.
Mark open neighbors when enqueuing them.

problems.title: Igor In the Museum
problems.brief: Answer how many picture-wall sides border the four-directional empty component of each queried museum cell. A picture can border it on multiple sides.
problems.target: O(rows*cols+q) time and O(rows*cols) space.
hints: Flood-fill each empty component once.
Count every neighboring wall side encountered.
Cache component IDs and totals for constant-time queries.

traps: DFS reachability does not guarantee a shortest path.
Counting cells instead of edges changes the initial distance.
A grid traversal can still need linear memory even when it changes cells in place.

steps: The start (0,0) is open and has path length 1.
Eight-direction movement allows the diagonal step to (1,1).
The destination is reached in the next BFS layer.

takeaway: BFS layers are shortest distances only when every step has the same cost.
