recall: Relate a tree’s level-order queue to a graph BFS queue, then explain why only the graph needs a visited rule.
javaTip: For queues of integer grid IDs, encode r*cols+c and decode with division and remainder; check the product fits int.
checklist: Use the correct direction set for each problem.
Test a blocked start and a one-cell open grid.
Explain why marking on enqueue avoids duplicate work.

title: Order dependencies and eliminate cycles
subtitle: Kahn’s algorithm and reverse safe-state processing
why: Indegree and outdegree counts let you reason about which work can happen now and which states can eventually terminate.
objectives: Derive a topological order with indegrees.
Detect when a directed cycle prevents completion.
Use reversed edges to propagate safety from terminal vertices.

lesson.title: Execute available work
lesson.body: A zero-indegree vertex has no remaining prerequisite. Remove it, append it to the order, and decrement the indegree of each outgoing neighbor.

lesson.title: Completion detects cycles
lesson.body: If fewer than V vertices are processed, some remaining vertices participate in or depend on directed cycles. A topological order exists only when all vertices are processed.

lesson.title: Reverse the viewpoint
lesson.body: For eventual safe states, begin with outdegree-zero vertices. On reversed edges, reduce each predecessor’s remaining outgoing count; it becomes safe when every outgoing route leads to safety.

problems.title: Course Schedule II
problems.brief: Return any valid order for all courses given prerequisite pairs, or an empty result if impossible. Include courses absent from all pairs.
problems.target: O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space.
hints: Interpret [course,prerequisite] as prerequisite→course.
Queue every vertex whose indegree is zero.
Check the processed count before returning the order.

problems.title: Find Eventual Safe States
problems.brief: In a directed graph, return vertices from which every possible path eventually terminates; return results in ascending vertex order.
problems.target: O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space, including a final linear scan of vertex labels.
hints: Start from terminal vertices.
Reverse all edges and track original outdegrees.
A predecessor becomes safe only when all of its outgoing edges have been eliminated.

problems.title: Fox And Names
problems.brief: Infer an alphabet order making the supplied lowercase names lexicographically sorted, or report impossibility.
problems.target: O(L+26^2) time and O(26^2) space, where L is total input length.
hints: For adjacent names, use only the first differing character.
Add that ordering edge; a longer word preceding its exact prefix is impossible.
Topologically sort all 26 letters and reject cycles.

traps: An undirected DSU cycle check cannot replace directed-cycle reasoning.
A node with one terminal route and one cyclic route is not safe.
If duplicate edges are retained, adjacency lists and degree counts must retain them consistently.

steps: Initial indegrees are [0,1,1,2], so start with 0.
Removing 0 makes both 1 and 2 available.
Removing 1 reduces indegree(3) to 1; removing 2 reduces it to 0.
Course 3 is processed last.

takeaway: A vertex becomes eligible only when every required dependency has been resolved.
recall: Explain why an ordinary BFS queue starts from one source while Kahn’s queue starts from every zero-indegree vertex.
javaTip: Use ArrayList<Integer>[] or lists of lists for adjacency; use ArrayDeque<Integer> unless lexicographic order explicitly requires a PriorityQueue.
checklist: Verify every returned edge goes forward in the order.
Test a self-loop and disconnected vertices.
Trace a safe-state graph containing both a terminal branch and a cycle.

title: Merge components and measure their size
subtitle: Redundant edges and the best single island flip
why: DSU separates component identity from component size, allowing both cycle detection and reasoning about a hypothetical connection.
objectives: Implement path compression and union by size.
Detect when an edge changes no component.
Sum distinct neighboring components for one land flip.

lesson.title: Represent a component
lesson.body: find(x) identifies a representative. Union by size attaches the smaller component to the larger; path compression shortens later searches.

lesson.title: Detect a redundant edge
lesson.body: Process undirected edges in order. If both endpoints already share a root, the edge adds a cycle to the current forest instead of connecting two components.

lesson.title: Evaluate one flip
lesson.body: For Making A Large Island, label existing islands or build their DSU components. For each zero, sum one plus the sizes of its distinct adjacent components; evaluate candidates without permanently merging every trial flip.

problems.title: Redundant Connection
problems.brief: An undirected graph began as a tree and received one extra edge. Return the edge whose removal restores a tree, following the problem’s input-order rule.
problems.target: O(E alpha(V)) time and O(V) space.
hints: Process edges in input order.
If find(u)==find(v), the new edge closes a cycle.
Otherwise union their components with a size or rank heuristic.

problems.title: Making A Large Island
problems.brief: Change at most one zero to one in an n×n binary grid to maximize a four-directionally connected island, with n<=500.
problems.target: O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space using component labels, or O(n^2*alpha(n^2)) with DSU.
hints: Label existing land components and record their sizes.
For each zero, add one plus the sizes of its distinct neighboring components.
Deduplicate neighboring component IDs and handle an already all-land grid.

problems.title: Roads not only in Berland
problems.brief: Replace redundant roads in an n-city network with n-1 roads to connect it without changing its road count. Print removals and replacements.
problems.target: O(n*alpha(n)) time and O(n) space.
hints: Use DSU to collect edges that fail to merge components.
Choose one representative of each remaining component.
Pair redundant-edge removals with new links between representatives.

traps: Two neighbors may belong to the same island and must be counted once.
An all-land grid already has area n*n.
Permanently applying every candidate flip would solve a different multi-flip problem.

steps: The diagonal land cells are two separate four-directional islands of size 1.
Flipping the upper-right zero connects both islands.
The resulting area is 1 for the flipped cell plus 1+1 from the distinct neighbors.

takeaway: A component’s representative identifies it; its size measures how much a new connection contributes.
recall: Contrast the successful-union condition with Kahn’s directed-cycle detection; they answer different graph questions.
javaTip: Encode a grid cell as row*n+col. Deduplicate the at most four neighboring roots before adding their sizes.
checklist: Return the redundant edge using failed union.
Test a zero touching the same island on several sides.
Handle all-zero and all-one grids.

title: Expand the cheapest frontier
subtitle: Dijkstra for additive and minimax costs
why: Weighted edges require a priority queue, and some problems change how path costs combine while preserving a useful monotonic ordering.
objectives: Use distance relaxation rather than a single visited flag.
Discard stale priority-queue entries.
Derive a minimax path transition.

lesson.title: Additive relaxation
lesson.body: A path through u improves v when dist[u]+weight(u,v)<dist[v]. Dijkstra is valid here because nonnegative weights cannot make a completed cheaper path worse later.

lesson.title: Lazy queue updates
lesson.body: Java priority queues do not decrease a key in place. Push a new entry after improvement and ignore an old entry when its stored distance no longer equals the best distance.

lesson.title: Minimax instead of sum
lesson.body: For minimum effort, a path’s cost is the largest edge difference encountered. Extending it gives max(currentEffort,edgeDifference), which never decreases the path cost.

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.brief: For a directed graph with nonnegative travel times, return how long a signal from source k takes to reach every vertex, or -1 if any is unreachable.
problems.target: O((V+E) log V) time with adjacency lists and a binary heap; O(V+E) space.
hints: Run single-source Dijkstra.
The answer is the largest final shortest distance.
Any vertex left at infinity makes the answer -1.

problems.title: Path With Minimum Effort
problems.brief: Move four-directionally through a height grid and minimize the largest absolute height difference along the path.
problems.target: O(rows×cols log(rows×cols)) time and O(rows×cols) space.
hints: Define path cost as a maximum, not a sum.
Relax a neighbor with max(currentEffort,abs(heightDifference)).
The first non-stale destination popped from the heap has minimum effort.

problems.title: Dijkstra?
problems.brief: Print a minimum-weight path from vertex 1 to n in a positive-weight undirected graph, or -1 if unreachable.
problems.target: O((V+E)*log(V+E)) time and O(V+E) space with a lazy heap.
hints: Run Dijkstra using long distances.
Store a predecessor whenever a relaxation improves a vertex.
Reconstruct backward from n and reverse the route.

traps: Ordinary Dijkstra does not support negative edge weights.
Marking a vertex final when it is merely inserted can discard a later shorter route.
Subtract heights in long before taking absolute value when input bounds can overflow int.

steps: Set dist[2]=0 and every other distance to infinity.
Relax from 2: dist[1]=1 and dist[3]=1.
Process 3 and set dist[4]=2.
Every vertex is reachable and the largest shortest distance is 2.

takeaway: Choose the path-combination rule before choosing the relaxation formula.
recall: Explain why BFS was sufficient for unit edges and why weighted edges change the frontier order.
javaTip: Use Long.compare for heap priorities; comparing by subtraction can overflow and violate the comparator contract.
checklist: Test an unreachable vertex and competing routes.
Demonstrate how a stale queue entry is ignored.
Contrast sum-cost and maximum-edge-cost relaxation.

title: Keep the resource limit in the path state
subtitle: Fee minimization under time limits and bounded flight counts
why: The cheapest arrival can leave too little time or too many used edges for a valid completion, so one scalar distance per city is insufficient.
objectives: Minimize fees while tracking elapsed time.
Convert stop limits into edge limits.
Use dependency order without reusing a bounded layer.

lesson.title: Price and time are different quantities
lesson.body: For Minimum Cost to Reach Destination in Time, dp[t][v] is the cheapest arrival at city v using exactly t time. Seed dp[0][0] with the source passing fee.

lesson.title: Positive time orders the states
lesson.body: For an edge taking w>0 time, read dp[t-w] and add the arrival city’s fee. Relax both directions of an undirected edge and minimize the destination over t<=maxTime.

lesson.title: Bounded flights use edge layers
lesson.body: At most K intermediate stops permits K+1 edges. Each Bellman–Ford-style pass reads the previous distance array and writes a separate next array, preventing several new edges from entering one layer.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Reach Destination in Time
problems.brief: Find the minimum total passing fees from city 0 to city n-1 within maxTime in an undirected graph. Pay a city’s fee each visit; travel times are positive and maxTime<=1000. Return -1 if unreachable.
problems.target: O(maxTime*(V+E)) time and O(maxTime*V) space with time-indexed DP.
hints: Use dp[time][city] for the cheapest exact-time arrival.
Seed dp[0][0] with the source fee and relax both directions of each edge from earlier times.
Add the arrival city’s fee and minimize destination states across all allowed times.

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.brief: Find the cheapest directed route with at most K intermediate stops, or -1 if none exists. Use nonnegative flight prices.
problems.target: O((K+1)(V+E)) time with copied bounded-edge layers and O(V) distance space.
hints: Convert the stop limit to K+1 edges.
Copy previous distances before each edge-relaxation pass.
Every relaxation must read from the previous array, not the next array.

problems.title: Shortest Path
problems.brief: Find a shortest undirected route from 1 to n that avoids every forbidden consecutive triple of vertices.
problems.target: O(V^2+sum(degree(v)^2)+F) time with pair-state BFS and hashed triples; O(V^2+F) space, excluding adjacency.
hints: Remember both previous and current vertices.
Begin BFS at (sentinel,1).
Reject (a,b)→(b,c) if forbidden; store parent states for reconstruction.

traps: The objective is minimum passing fees, not minimum travel time.
Pay the source fee and every arrival fee; do not forget a revisited city.
In-place bounded-flight relaxation can exceed the allowed edge count.

steps: The direct 0→2 route costs fees 1+3=4 but takes 20 time, so it is invalid.
Route 0→1→2 takes 5+5=10 time.
Its fees are 1+2+3=6 and it meets the time limit.
dryRun.answer: 6. The unconstrained cheapest route is not feasible.

takeaway: Store the resource that controls future feasibility separately from the quantity being optimized.
recall: Explain why one cheapest-fee distance per city loses time-budget information, then contrast elapsed-time states with bounded-flight edge layers.
javaTip: Allocate a time-by-city table only after checking its size; guard INF before adding fees and keep separate arrays for bounded flight passes.
checklist: Test a cheap route that exceeds the time limit.
Test unreachable destinations and K=0 flights.
Explain why positive edge times allow increasing-time DP.

title: Model the state graph before searching it
subtitle: Alternating colors and obstacle budgets
why: This checkpoint uses BFS on expanded states: the physical cell or vertex alone no longer determines legal next moves.
objectives: Derive a state from the next-move restriction.
Keep visitation separate for different resource states.
Choose BFS when every expanded-state transition still costs one.

lesson.title: Last color changes the next edge
lesson.body: For alternating paths, store the vertex and last edge color. The same vertex may need to be processed twice, once for each last-color possibility.

lesson.title: Remaining eliminations change reachability
lesson.body: In an obstacle grid, a state is row, column, and remaining budget. Arriving with more eliminations left can unlock a path unavailable to an earlier state.

lesson.title: Distance is still a BFS layer
lesson.body: Although the state graph is larger, each move costs one edge. BFS remains correct; Dijkstra adds no value unless step costs differ.

problems.title: Shortest Path with Alternating Colors
problems.brief: For a directed graph with red and blue edges, find shortest distances from vertex 0 where consecutive edge colors alternate; either color may be first.
problems.target: O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space across two color states per vertex.
hints: Track a separate distance for each last color.
Initialize source states so either first color is allowed.
From a red-last state, traverse only blue edges, and vice versa.

problems.title: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination
problems.brief: In a four-directional binary grid with open start and end, eliminate at most K obstacle cells and minimize moves to the destination.
problems.target: O(rows×cols×(K+1)) time and space for a direct state-BFS solution.
hints: Store remaining eliminations with the position.
Entering an obstacle consumes one unit; reject negative remaining budgets.
Use visited[row][col][remaining], not only visited[row][col].

problems.title: Directing Edges
problems.brief: Orient undirected edges of a mixed graph to make the final graph acyclic, preserving fixed directed edges, or report impossibility.
problems.target: O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space.
hints: Topologically sort using fixed directed edges only.
A cycle among fixed edges cannot be repaired.
Orient remaining edges from earlier to later in that order.

traps: The same vertex with different last colors is not the same state.
Grid path length here counts moves, unlike the cell-count convention on day 49.
A visited flag for location alone can reject a useful arrival with more remaining budget.

dryRun.input: Vertices 0,1,2; red edges 0→1 and 1→2; blue edge 1→2
steps: Vertex 0 starts at distance 0 with either first color permitted.
Take red 0→1, reaching state (1,lastRed) at distance 1.
From that state the red 1→2 is forbidden, but the blue 1→2 is allowed.

takeaway: The smallest correct search state remembers exactly what determines the next legal move.
recall: Compare coupon-state Dijkstra with color-state BFS and explain why their frontier structures differ.
javaTip: Represent small states with an int record or compact int[]; keep color indices named constants to avoid swapped transitions.
checklist: Trace two arrivals at one cell with different obstacle budgets.
Test self-loops, parallel colored edges, and unreachable vertices.
Justify the number of states before allocating visited storage.

title: First full assessment and error diagnosis
subtitle: Window counting, subset feasibility, and a timed mock
why: You now have the main tools. This assessment measures recognition, implementation reliability, and time allocation, then turns failures into repair tasks.
objectives: Select an approach from constraints without topic labels.
Protect complete solutions during a timed session.
Classify every failure by its cause.

lesson.title: Review two recognition patterns
lesson.body: Before the mock, explain why exactly-K distinct counts use two at-most windows and why equal-sum partition uses a bounded subset state.

lesson.title: Run the mock without editorial access
lesson.body: Use three unseen questions with array/string, DP, and tree/graph coverage. The 180-minute format is a practice choice, not a universal claim about every Infosys assessment.

lesson.title: Turn the score into evidence
lesson.body: Record time spent reading, coding, and debugging. Label misses as recognition, recurrence, complexity, implementation, or test coverage; choose one concrete repair for each.

problems.title: Count Number of Nice Subarrays
problems.brief: Count contiguous subarrays with exactly k odd numbers; only parity affects the state.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space with prefix-odd frequencies.
hints: Conceptually replace odd values by one and even values by zero.
At prefix odd-count p, add earlier prefix counts at p-k.
Seed count[0]=1 and query before recording the new prefix.

problems.title: Profitable Schemes
problems.brief: Count job subsets using at most n workers and earning at least minProfit, modulo 1,000,000,007. Each job is used once and both thresholds are at most 100.
problems.target: O(jobs*(n+1)*(minProfit+1)) time and O((n+1)*(minProfit+1)) space.
hints: Cap accumulated profit at minProfit.
Use workersUsed and cappedProfit with dp[0][0]=1.
Process with descending worker counts or a fresh layer; sum all feasible worker counts at the profit threshold.

problems.title: Colored Rectangles
problems.brief: Pair rectangles of different colors for product scores, using each at most once. Maximize the total across three collections of at most 200 rectangles each.
problems.target: O((R+1)*(G+1)*(B+1)) time and space with three-count DP.
hints: Sort colors and consume their largest available values.
Track how many rectangles have been consumed from each color.
Try all three color-pair choices when available; retain the best reachable score.

traps: Do not infer a role or offer level from a mock’s solved count.
Spending the full session on one hard problem hides which other questions you could finish.
An accepted revision problem does not substitute for the unseen timed set.

steps: atMost(2) counts 12 subarrays.
atMost(1) counts only the five single-element subarrays, so it is 5.
The difference isolates exactly two distinct values.

takeaway: An error log should tell you what to change in the next attempt.
recall: Name one invariant from arrays, one DP state, and one graph state before beginning the mock.
javaTip: Prepare a minimal Java input/output skeleton before starting the timer; print no debug output in final submissions.
checklist: Finish a 180-minute unseen three-question mock.
Save each failing input with the bug category.
Choose the single highest-impact weakness to repair on day 56.

mock.brief: Use today’s three assigned problems as a 180-minute mock if they are unseen. Otherwise choose three unseen replacements at similar levels. Read all statements first, allocate your time, and save the last 15 minutes for edge cases and submission checks.

title: Repair subarray counting assumptions
subtitle: Positive threshold windows and repeated binary-prefix sums
why: Finding one shortest valid window and counting every exact-sum subarray require different accounting, especially when zeroes create repeated prefix sums.
objectives: Prove the threshold window’s monotonicity.
Count binary exact sums with prefix frequencies.
Use the first mock’s failure log to build targeted counterexamples.

lesson.title: Find a shortest positive window
lesson.body: With positive values and a positive target, expand until the sum reaches the threshold, then shrink while it remains valid. Record the shortest length during shrinking.

lesson.title: Count all exact binary sums
lesson.body: A subarray sums to goal when currentPrefix-earlierPrefix=goal. Count all earlier prefixes equal to currentPrefix-goal, then record the current prefix.

lesson.title: Zeroes preserve multiple starts
lesson.body: Zeroes do not break sum monotonicity, but they make several starts share the same prefix sum. A frequency table retains all of them; a set does not. An at-most difference is another valid counting approach.

problems.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
problems.brief: For positive integers and a positive target, return the smallest length of a subarray with sum at least target, or zero if none exists.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Expand until the sum reaches the threshold.
While valid, update the answer and remove the left value.
The positivity assumption guarantees the window movement is safe.

problems.title: Binary Subarrays With Sum
problems.brief: Count subarrays of a binary array summing to goal, including goal zero and long zero runs.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) space with prefix-sum frequencies.
hints: Binary prefix sums lie between zero and n.
Before recording prefix p, add earlier occurrences of p-goal.
Keep frequencies rather than a set because repeated sums represent different starts.

problems.title: Cleaning the Phone
problems.brief: Free at least m memory by removing phone apps with inconvenience one or two. Minimize inconvenience, or return -1.
problems.target: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
hints: Split sizes by cost and sort each group descending.
Fix the removed cost-one count and compute the remaining memory need.
Binary-search the smallest sufficient cost-two prefix and minimize i+2*j.

traps: A shortest-window result does not count all valid subarrays.
Repeated prefix sums need frequencies, not presence flags.
For goal=0, recording the current prefix before querying incorrectly includes an empty subarray.

steps: Seed prefix frequency 0 with one occurrence.
After the first 1 and 0, prefix 1 has frequency 2 and no answer has appeared.
The next 1 gives prefix 2 and adds one answer; the next 0 repeats prefix 2 and adds another.
The final 1 gives prefix 3; its two earlier prefix-1 occurrences add two answers.

takeaway: Choose the state and counting rule from the requested answer, not only from the word subarray.
recall: Reopen one failed mock problem, name its mistaken assumption, and reimplement it after these two contrast drills.
javaTip: Binary prefix sums lie in [0,n], so int[] frequencies avoid hashing; use long for a reusable subarray-count result.
checklist: Pass the minimum-window threshold boundary cases.
Test binary goal zero and an all-zero array.
Re-solve one mock failure from a blank Java file.

title: Combine restrictions without losing the state
subtitle: Fixed windows, tie-breaking, and key-dependent movement
why: These problems combine familiar components with one extra requirement that a generic template often misses.
objectives: Enforce lexicographic tie-breaking deliberately.
Combine position with a collected-key mask.
Estimate the full state count from the key limit.

lesson.title: Separate three fixed windows
lesson.body: For three nonoverlapping windows of equal length K, precompute window sums. A left-best and right-best array lets each middle window choose its best legal neighbors in constant time.

lesson.title: Tie-breaking is part of correctness
lesson.body: When sums tie, prefer the lexicographically smallest triple of start indices. The direction of scans and the strictness of comparisons must preserve earlier indices.

lesson.title: Movement depends on inventory
lesson.body: For a key-and-lock grid, the visited state includes the collected-key mask. A cell that was blocked by a lock can become reachable after the corresponding key is collected.

problems.title: Maximum Sum of 3 Non-Overlapping Subarrays
problems.brief: For positive values and n>=3K, choose three length-K subarrays maximizing total sum; return the lexicographically smallest start-index triple on ties.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.
hints: Precompute every length-K window sum.
Store the best legal left and right windows for each middle candidate.
On equal sums, keep the earliest left/right starts and compare final triples consistently.

problems.title: Shortest Path to Get All Keys
problems.brief: Move four-directionally through a grid with walls, at most six keys, and matching locks. Find the fewest moves needed to collect every key.
problems.target: O(rows×cols×2^k) time and space, where k<=6 is the number of keys after compact indexing.
hints: Scan once to identify keys and the goal mask.
Use BFS on (row,col,keyMask).
A lock is traversable only when its key bit is already present; collecting a key updates the mask.

problems.title: Alyona and Strings
problems.brief: Choose exactly k nonempty nonoverlapping common substring blocks in two strings, in order, maximizing total matched length.
problems.target: O(n*m*k) time and O(m*k) rolling-row space with an inside-block state.
hints: Track both best prefixes and a matching block ending at the current character pair.
Equal characters extend a block or start one from a k-1-block prefix.
Skip characters only between blocks and keep impossible exact counts unreachable.

traps: A maximum-sum answer can still fail if its tied indices are not lexicographically smallest.
For three windows, use starts that guarantee disjoint ranges.
Marking only the grid position visited prevents returning with newly acquired keys.

steps: Length-two sums are [3,3,3,8,13,12,6].
For middle start 3, choose left start 0 with sum 3 and right start 5 with sum 12.
The resulting total is 3+8+12=23.
Another total-23 triple exists, but [0,3,5] is lexicographically smaller.

takeaway: An extra tie rule or resource variable belongs in the correctness proof.
recall: Explain how a key mask resembles assignment DP’s mask and how BFS supplies the evaluation order here.
javaTip: For keys, build a char-to-bit index map or use the actual a–f bit positions consistently with the goal mask; do not assume a missing letter is present.
checklist: Verify lexicographic ties on equal-valued arrays.
Trace revisiting a cell after collecting a key.
Write state-count and memory estimates before coding.

title: Second assessment under realistic constraints
subtitle: LIS, weighted paths, and time-budget repair
why: This mock tests whether your repairs survive time pressure and whether you can select an optimization based on input size.
objectives: Choose O(n²) versus O(n log n) from bounds.
Apply Dijkstra with correct queue discipline.
Compare the second mock’s error categories with the first.

lesson.title: Warm up the decision, not the memory
lesson.body: For LIS, justify strict lower-bound behavior. For weighted routes, justify why BFS is insufficient and how stale priority-queue entries are handled.

lesson.title: Adjust your allocation rule
lesson.body: Use day 55’s evidence to decide when to park a stuck problem. Record the reason for switching rather than moving randomly between questions.

lesson.title: Evaluate repair effectiveness
lesson.body: After the mock, compare recurring bug types and time losses. A repeated failure deserves a smaller focused example on day 59 before another full solution attempt.

problems.title: Russian Doll Envelopes
problems.brief: Find the longest chain with both width and height strictly increasing. Rotation is forbidden and equal widths cannot nest.
problems.target: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
hints: Sort widths ascending and tied heights descending.
This tie order prevents increasing-height subsequences from choosing two equal-width envelopes.
Run strict LIS on heights using the first tail greater than or equal to the new height.

problems.title: Reachable Nodes In Subdivided Graph
problems.brief: Edges contain specified intermediate nodes. From node 0 within maxMoves steps, count reachable original and intermediate nodes without expanding the graph.
problems.target: O((V+E) log V) time and O(V+E) space.
hints: An edge with c intermediate nodes has endpoint travel cost c+1.
Run Dijkstra to determine remaining moves at original endpoints.
For each edge add min(c,remainingFromU+remainingFromV), avoiding double-counting.

problems.title: Planets
problems.brief: Find earliest arrival through a weighted undirected graph whose vertices have forbidden departure times. Waiting is allowed; the destination needs no departure.
problems.target: O((V+E)*log(V+E)+B) expected time after preprocessing B sorted blocked times; O(V+E+B) space.
hints: Map blocked times in each consecutive run to the first allowed time after it.
After finalizing arrival at a vertex, apply departure waiting before relaxing edges.
Return destination arrival without waiting there.

traps: A smaller tails value does not mean the tails array is itself the reconstructed LIS.
A reachable subset of vertices is insufficient for the network-delay answer.
Use unseen mock questions; memorized solutions hide recognition weaknesses.

steps: Read 0 and 1: tails=[0,1].
The next 0 replaces the first tail, leaving length 2.
Read 3: tails=[0,1,3]; read 2: tails=[0,1,2].
The final 3 extends tails to [0,1,2,3].

takeaway: The second mock should show fewer repeated mistakes, not merely a different score.
recall: Before the timer, name the error you repaired on day 56 and the test that now catches it.
javaTip: Use one small immutable heap-state class or record with vertex and distance; never mutate a queued object’s comparison key.
checklist: Complete a second unseen 180-minute mock.
Compare repeated error categories against day 55.
Select two concrete failure cases for day 59 repair.

mock.brief: Use today’s three assigned problems as a 180-minute mock if they are unseen. Otherwise choose three unseen replacements at similar levels. Read all statements first, allocate your time, and save the last 15 minutes for edge cases and submission checks.

title: Repair boundary states and prove the fix
subtitle: All-negative paths, empty prefixes, and regression cases
why: Today focuses on defects that survive ordinary examples: invalid default values, unreset state, and incorrect empty-input meaning.
objectives: Make nonempty-answer requirements explicit.
Validate base rows and columns before transitions.
Turn mock failures into reusable regression inputs.

lesson.title: A default can change the problem
lesson.body: A zero-initialized best path allows an empty answer. For a nonempty maximum-path problem, initialize the answer to the smallest allowed result and consider each node.

lesson.title: Empty prefixes are meaningful states
lesson.body: In Edit Distance, converting a length-i prefix to empty takes i deletions. Those base states are not special exceptions; every later insertion or deletion depends on them.

lesson.title: Repair the mechanism
lesson.body: For each day-58 failure, write the violated invariant, the smallest reproducing input, and the changed rule. Rerun the original failure after the small case passes.

problems.title: Maximum Product of Splitted Binary Tree
problems.brief: Remove one edge from a positive-valued binary tree to maximize the product of the component sums. Apply modulo 1,000,000,007 only after maximizing.
problems.target: O(n) time and O(h) recursive auxiliary space.
hints: Compute the entire tree’s sum first.
Each non-root subtree sum s gives s*(total-s).
Compare full long products before applying the modulus.

problems.title: Minimum ASCII Delete Sum for Two Strings
problems.brief: Delete characters until two strings become equal, minimizing the total deleted ASCII value while preserving order.
problems.target: O(nm) time and O(min(n,m)) rolling-row space.
hints: Empty-prefix boundaries cost the sum of deleted codes.
Matching final characters can both remain, using the diagonal.
Otherwise compare deleting the final character from either prefix and add its code.

problems.title: Linova and Kingdom
problems.brief: Choose k industry vertices maximizing happiness from non-industry ancestors along their root routes.
problems.target: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
hints: Compute depth and subtree size.
Use benefit[u]=depth[u]-(subtreeSize[u]-1).
Sort and sum the largest k benefits, explaining what the subtree penalty removes.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick
problems.brief: Cut a stick at all requested interior positions in any order. Every cut costs the current segment length; minimize the total with at most 100 cuts.

problems.brief: Change direction arrows in a grid at one cost per changed cell to enable a top-left to bottom-right path with minimum total changes.
